text: Unless an entry says otherwise:
A failing function returns a sentinel (-1, `NULL`, `EOF`, `(size_t)-1`, `MAP_FAILED`, ...) and stores a positive error code in the calling thread's `errno`.

`errno` is never set to 0 by a library function. A successful call may still change `errno`. ⚑ HIST: callers that need to detect errors from functions with no free sentinel (for example `strtol`, `readdir`, `getpwnam`, math functions) must zero `errno` before the call. An explicit status result would remove that burden.

The error codes are the kernel's (`EPERM`=1 ... `EHWPOISON`=133 on x86_64). ⚑ KERN: the numbering is the kernel ABI. Library-originated failures reuse kernel codes with library meanings (for example `EINVAL`, `ENOMEM`, `EOVERFLOW`).

Newer POSIX interfaces (threads, `posix_spawn`, `posix_fadvise`, `posix_fallocate`, `posix_memalign`, `getaddrinfo`, `pthread_*`, `timer_*` are mixed) return the error number directly and leave `errno` unspecified. ⚑ PATH: two error conventions coexist in one library. A caller must know which convention each function follows.

Unless stated, functions are *MT-Safe* in the manual's terminology (§1.2.2.1 of the manual defines MT-Safe, MT-Unsafe, AS-Safe, AC-Safe with qualifiers such as `race`, `locale`, `env`, `sig`, `term`, `init`, `lock`, `corrupt`, `heap`, `dlopen`, `plugin`, `i18n`, `timer`). The specification lists only departures:

**Static result buffers.** Many classic functions return a pointer to storage owned by the library and overwritten by the next call (`strerror` historically, `asctime`, `ctime`, `gmtime`, `localtime`, `getpwnam`, `gethostbyname`, `inet_ntoa`, `ttyname`, `strtok`, `readdir`, `getlogin`, `ecvt`, `l64a`, `tmpnam(NULL)`, `ptsname`, ...). ⚑ HIST, ⚑ PATH: each of these grew a `_r` variant taking a caller buffer. The functional need is always "produce a result the caller owns", so in a new design the `_r` shape is the base contract.

**Process-global mutable state that the contract exposes.** The current locale, the environment, the current directory, `umask`, signal dispositions, resource limits, the random seed of `rand`/`random`/`drand48`, the `getopt` cursor (`optind`, `optarg`), the `strtok` cursor, `h_errno`, `signgam`, the `tzname`/`timezone`/`daylight` variables, `environ`, `program_invocation_name`. Several of these are kernel-held (cwd, umask, signal dispositions, limits) and cannot be made per-thread. The others are library-held and are process-global only for history.

**Async-signal safety.** Only functions listed as AS-Safe may be called from a signal handler that interrupted arbitrary code. POSIX enumerates the list. The functional reason is that the handler may run in the middle of a non-reentrant library operation on the same thread.

**Cancellation points.** In a threaded program, the functions POSIX lists as cancellation points (blocking I/O, waits, sleeps, `open`, `close`, ...) may act on a pending deferred cancellation. glibc's cancellable wrappers are listed per section. ⚑ HIST: `close` being a cancellation point creates a well-known ambiguity about whether the descriptor was closed (on Linux it always is).

Blocking primitives interrupted by a signal handler either restart automatically (handler installed with `SA_RESTART`) or fail with `EINTR`. Some kernel calls never restart (`select`, `poll`, `epoll_wait`, `nanosleep`, `sigsuspend`, socket calls with timeouts, ...) and some restart with an adjusted timeout. glibc does not hide this, apart from a few internal `TEMP_FAILURE_RETRY` loops. ⚑ KERN (restart semantics are kernel ABI), ⚑ HIST (`EINTR` as a caller-visible result is widely considered a design mistake, but the kernel ABI returns it).

On x86_64, `off_t`, `ino_t`, `blkcnt_t`, `rlim_t`, and `time_t` are already 64 bits. The `*64` symbols (`open64`, `stat64`, `lseek64`, `fopen64`, `readdir64`, `getrlimit64`, ...) are exact aliases of the unsuffixed symbols. ⚑ COMPAT: they exist because on 32-bit ABIs `_FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64` and `_TIME_BITS=64` select 64-bit variants of hundreds of functions. The specification documents each function once. The 64-bit variant is the contract, and the 32-bit variant is a compatibility shim that must fail with `EOVERFLOW` when a value does not fit.

Symbols named `__<name>_chk` (`__memcpy_chk`, `__printf_chk`, `__read_chk`, ...) implement the same contract as `<name>` with one extra input: the compiler-known size of the destination object. If the operation would write beyond it, the process terminates with a diagnostic (`__chk_fail`, "buffer overflow detected"). Format-string variants also reject `%n` in writable memory. ⚑ PATH: fortification is needed because the base interfaces do not take destination sizes. An interface that always carried a destination extent would make the whole `_chk` family unnecessary.

Every exported name carries a version node (`GLIBC_2.2.5` is the x86_64 baseline). Some names have several versions with different contracts (for example `memcpy@GLIBC_2.2.5` permits overlapping arguments, while `memcpy@GLIBC_2.14` does not guarantee it; `realpath`, `sched_setaffinity`, `pthread_cond_*`, `regexec`, `glob`, `posix_spawn`, `nftw`, `fmemopen`, `quick_exit` all have older versioned contracts). Some names are exported only for old binaries and can no longer be linked against (`gets`, `matherr`, `__malloc_hook`, `sys_errlist`, `pow10`, `sigvec`, `ustat`, `stime`, `_sys_siglist`, the RPC/NIS stack moved to `libtirpc`/`libnsl`, ...). ⚑ COMPAT: an ABI-compatible replacement must keep every versioned contract that old binaries were linked against. Appendix B lists these.

Unless stated, pointers the caller passes are borrowed only for the call's duration. Pointers the library returns are either (a) caller-owned heap memory to be released with `free`, (b) library-owned static storage (see C0.2), or (c) a view into caller-supplied storage. Each entry states which. ⚑ HIST: the C interface does not encode ownership in types, and several functions return different kinds from the same entry point (`realpath` with and without a buffer, `getcwd(NULL, 0)`, `strerror_r` GNU form).
The kernel ABI that glibc builds on includes more than syscall numbers:
The process entry state: stack layout (`argc`, `argv`, `envp`, auxiliary vector), initial register state.

The **auxiliary vector** (`AT_PAGESZ`, `AT_HWCAP`/`AT_HWCAP2`, `AT_RANDOM`, `AT_SYSINFO_EHDR`, `AT_SECURE`, `AT_PHDR`, `AT_ENTRY`, `AT_BASE`, `AT_MINSIGSTKSZ`, `AT_EXECFN`, `AT_PLATFORM`, `AT_CLKTCK`, `AT_UID`/`AT_EUID`/`AT_GID`/`AT_EGID`).
The **vDSO**: `clock_gettime`, `gettimeofday`, `time`, `getcpu`, `clock_getres`.
The **signal frame** format and the `SA_RESTORER` / `rt_sigreturn` convention (x86_64 requires user space to supply the return trampoline).
The **thread pointer** register (FS base on x86_64, set through `arch_prctl(ARCH_SET_FS)` or `clone(CLONE_SETTLS)`).
**Shared user/kernel memory protocols**: futex words, robust-futex lists (`set_robust_list`), `clear_child_tid` (`set_tid_address` / `CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID`), and the rseq area (`rseq`).

**Pseudo-file systems**: `/proc` (`/proc/self/fd`, `/proc/self/maps`, `/proc/self/exe`, `/proc/stat`, `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/sys/...`), `/sys` (`/sys/devices/system/cpu/...`), and `/dev` nodes (`/dev/ptmx`, `/dev/pts/*`, `/dev/null`, `/dev/tty`, `/dev/shm` for POSIX shared memory (a tmpfs mount convention), `/dev/log` (a syslog daemon socket, not kernel)).
**Netlink** (`NETLINK_ROUTE`) for interface and address enumeration. Appendix A catalogues all of these against the contracts that need them.
Before `main` runs, the runtime turns the kernel's entry state into a C execution environment:
It passes `argc`, `argv`, and `envp`.
It makes the environment available as `environ`.
It initializes the thread pointer and TLS for the initial thread, and the stack-protector canary and pointer-guard values from `AT_RANDOM`.
It initializes the standard streams `stdin`, `stdout` and `stderr`, and the "C" locale.
It runs ELF constructors (`DT_PREINIT_ARRAY`, `DT_INIT`, `DT_INIT_ARRAY`) in dependency order.
It registers destructors to run at normal exit.
In secure-execution mode (`AT_SECURE` non-zero, which means setuid, setgid or file-capability binaries), it sanitizes the environment.
`argv[argc]` is `NULL`.
`envp` is `NULL`-terminated.

Descriptors 0, 1 and 2 are open when `main` runs. For secure-mode programs, glibc opens `/dev/null` on any of 0, 1, 2 that are closed. This prevents a privileged program's later `open` from receiving fd 1 or 2 and having its diagnostics written into a sensitive file.

In secure mode, unsafe environment variables are removed (`LD_PRELOAD`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `GCONV_PATH`, `LOCPATH`, `MALLOC_*`, `TMPDIR`, `NLSPATH`, `HOSTALIASES`, `RES_OPTIONS`, `GLIBC_TUNABLES` with unsafe tunables, ...).

**`exit(status)`** runs, in reverse order of registration, all functions registered with `atexit`, `on_exit` and `__cxa_atexit`. Registrations made during exit processing also run. It then runs thread-local destructors for the calling thread, ELF destructors (`DT_FINI_ARRAY`) of loaded objects, flushes and closes all stdio streams, removes `tmpfile` files, and terminates the whole process with the status. It never returns.
**`_exit`/`_Exit(status)`** terminate the process immediately. They skip handlers, stream flushing and destructors. Async-signal-safe.
**`quick_exit(status)`** runs only the `at_quick_exit` handlers (LIFO), then `_Exit`.
**`abort()`** terminates abnormally with `SIGABRT`:
If a handler catches `SIGABRT` and returns, `abort` resets the disposition to default and raises the signal again.
If the process still survives, it executes an architecture trap instruction and finally `_exit(127)`.
The raise is not blocked by the signal mask: `abort` unblocks `SIGABRT` first.
Streams are *not* flushed (POSIX.1-2008 permits but no longer requires flushing; glibc stopped flushing in 2.27).
**`__cxa_atexit(fn, arg, dso)`** registers a destructor bound to a shared object. `__cxa_finalize(dso)` runs that object's destructors when it is unloaded (or all of them at exit when `dso` is NULL).
**`__cxa_thread_atexit_impl(fn, obj, dso)`** registers a destructor for a C++ `thread_local` object. It runs at thread exit, and it keeps `dso` loaded until then.
**`status`** is an `int`. Only the low 8 bits reach a parent through `wait` (⚑ KERN: `exit_group` takes an int, but the wait-status encoding carries 8 bits).
**`EXIT_SUCCESS`/`EXIT_FAILURE`** are 0 and 1.
Registration limit: ISO C requires at least 32 `atexit` registrations. glibc has no fixed limit and allocates dynamically.
`atexit`, `at_quick_exit` and `__cxa_atexit` return non-zero if memory cannot be obtained.
Calling `exit` twice, or from an `atexit` handler, is undefined in ISO C. glibc detects reentry: later handlers are still run once.
`exit` from a multi-threaded process terminates all threads without running their cleanup handlers.
The process environment is a mutable mapping from names to values. It is initialized from `execve`'s `envp` and passed to children by the `exec*` functions that do not take an explicit environment.
**`getenv(name)`** returns the value for `name`, or `NULL` if absent.
**`secure_getenv(name)`** behaves like `getenv`, but returns `NULL` in secure-execution mode.
**`setenv(name, value, overwrite)`** adds or (if `overwrite`) replaces an entry.
**`unsetenv(name)`** removes *all* entries with that name.
**`putenv(string)`** inserts the caller's `NAME=VALUE` string itself (not a copy). Later changes to that storage change the environment. A string with no `=` removes the name (glibc extension).
**`clearenv()`** empties the environment.
A name must be non-empty and must not contain `=`. `setenv` and `unsetenv` fail with `EINVAL` otherwise.
Names and values are Text. They cannot contain the delimiter because the storage format is `NAME=VALUE\0` (⚑ KERN at `execve`, ⚑ HIST in memory).
`getenv`'s result stays valid until the entry is modified or removed.
`setenv` copies its arguments.
`ENOMEM`.
`EINVAL` for a bad name.
Duplicate names that came from `execve` are all removed by `unsetenv`. `getenv` returns the first.

MT-Unsafe `env`. Concurrent `getenv` and `setenv` are a data race. ⚑ HIST: `environ` is a bare global array that callers may read or replace directly, so the library cannot synchronize access. The functional need, a process-wide name→value map inherited across `exec`, would permit a lock-protected or copy-on-write structure. The catch is that `environ` is ABI.
Provides the `argv[0]` of the running program, both in full and as its final path component, for diagnostics.
Returns the value of an auxiliary-vector entry the kernel supplied at `execve`.
A key (`AT_*`, `unsigned long`).
Returns the value if present.
Returns 0 and sets `ENOENT` if absent. ⚑ ARB: 0 is also a legitimate value for several keys, so the caller must inspect `errno`.

Iteratively classifies the elements of an argument list into options, option arguments and operands, according to a short-option specification string and (for the long forms) a table of long-option descriptors.
**The argument list** (`argc`, `argv`).

**The short-option specification**, a Text in which each character is an option letter, `:` after it means a required argument, and `::` means an optional one. A leading `+` requests POSIX mode (stop at the first operand). A leading `-` returns operands in place as option code 1. A leading `:` suppresses diagnostics and distinguishes a missing argument (`:`) from an unknown option (`?`).
**The long-option table** (`struct option {name, has_arg, flag, val}`), terminated by an all-zero entry.
Each call returns the next option's code, or -1 when options are exhausted.
`optarg` points at the option's argument.
`optind` is the index of the next element to process.
By default (GNU mode), `getopt` **permutes** `argv` so that all operands end up at the end. Setting `POSIXLY_CORRECT` disables permutation.
`--` ends option processing.
An unknown option, or a missing required argument, returns `'?'` (or `':'`) and prints a diagnostic to `stderr` unless `opterr == 0`.
A long option may be abbreviated to any unambiguous prefix. An ambiguous prefix is an error.

Parse a comma-separated option Text (`"rw,size=10"`) against a NULL-terminated list of recognized names. Each call returns the index of the next suboption, or -1 if it is unknown, and sets a pointer to its `=value` (or `NULL`); for an unknown suboption the pointer is the whole `name[=value]` text. The input is modified in place (commas and `=` are overwritten with terminators) and a cursor is advanced.
A declarative command-line parser. The caller supplies a tree of option tables (`struct argp`, which may nest child parsers) and a callback. The library:
parses the list and calls the callback for each option, each operand, and the initialization/finalization events;
generates `--help`, `--usage` and `--version` output, formatted to the terminal width (`ARGP_HELP_FMT` tunes this);
reports errors in the standard `program: message` format.
Option descriptors (`name`, `key`, `arg`, `flags`, `doc`, `group`). Flags such as `ARGP_NO_EXIT`, `ARGP_IN_ORDER`, `ARGP_NO_HELP`, `ARGP_PARSE_ARGV0`, `ARGP_SILENT`.
On success returns 0 and optionally the index of the first unparsed argument. By default the process exits with `argp_err_exit_status` (default `EX_USAGE`) on a usage error.
An error code returned from the callback aborts the parse. `ARGP_ERR_UNKNOWN` means "not mine; try child parsers".

The `GLIBC_TUNABLES` environment variable (`name=value:name=value`) adjusts library parameters at startup: malloc arena counts and thresholds, tcache sizes, thread stack cache, CPU feature masks (`glibc.cpu.hwcaps`), `glibc.rtld.*`, `glibc.pthread.rseq`, and others. Unknown or invalid tunables are ignored. In secure-execution mode, only tunables marked safe are honoured.
A per-thread modifiable integer lvalue that holds the most recent error code set by a library function on this thread. `errno` is a macro that expands to `(*__errno_location())`.
Each thread has its own `errno`, and signal handlers see the interrupted thread's `errno`. Portable handlers save and restore it.
Map an error number to a message.

**`strerror(e)`** returns a locale-translated message. The result is a pointer that stays valid until the next `strerror` call on the same thread (glibc uses a per-thread buffer only for unknown codes; known codes return a static string).
**`strerror_l(e, loc)`** does the same using locale object `loc`.
**`strerror_r(e, buf, n)`** has two contracts selected by feature macro (§0.5):
**XSI form (`__xpg_strerror_r`)** writes into `buf` and returns 0, `EINVAL` (unknown `e`) or `ERANGE` (buffer too small).
**GNU form** returns a `char *` that *may or may not* point into `buf` (it points at a static string for known codes).
**`strerrorname_np(e)`** returns the symbolic name (`"EINVAL"`), or `NULL` for an unknown code.
**`strerrordesc_np(e)`** returns the untranslated English description.
**`perror(s)`** writes `s: <message>\n` (or just the message if `s` is NULL or empty) to `stderr`. If `stderr` is unoriented, it makes it byte-oriented; it honours the orientation if already set.
Unknown codes yield `"Unknown error N"`.
Print `progname: <formatted message>[: <strerror(errno)>]\n` to `stderr`.
`err*` then call `exit(status)`.
`error(status, errnum, fmt, ...)` exits if `status != 0`. It includes the message for `errnum` if non-zero, flushes `stdout` first, and counts messages in `error_message_count`.
`error_at_line` additionally prints `file:line:`. With `error_one_per_line`, it suppresses repeated messages for the same line.
`error_print_progname`, if set, replaces the program-name prefix.

If the asserted expression is false and `NDEBUG` is not defined, print `prog: file:line: function: Assertion 'expr' failed.` and call `abort`. `assert_perror(e)` (GNU) does the same when `e != 0`, showing `strerror(e)`.
**`__stack_chk_fail`** is called by compiler-inserted code when a stack canary has changed. It prints `*** stack smashing detected ***: terminated` and aborts.
**`__chk_fail`** is called when a fortified function detects an overflow (C0.5). It prints `*** buffer overflow detected ***: terminated` and aborts.
No return. The diagnostic uses only async-signal-safe output, so it is written even from a corrupted heap state.
Formats a structured message from these fields and writes it to `stderr`, the console, or both:
**classification**: `MM_HARD`/`MM_SOFT`/`MM_FIRM`, `MM_APPL`/`MM_UTIL`/`MM_OPSYS`, `MM_RECOVER`/`MM_NRECOV`, `MM_PRINT`/`MM_CONSOLE`;
**label**: `"xxx:yyy"`, a component and subcomponent of at most 10 and 14 characters;
**severity**: `MM_HALT`, `MM_ERROR`, `MM_WARNING`, `MM_INFO`, or a severity added with `addseverity`;
**text**, **action**, **tag**. `MSGVERB` selects the fields to print and `SEV_LEVEL` defines extra severities.
Returns `MM_OK`, `MM_NOTOK`, `MM_NOMSG` (stderr failed) or `MM_NOCON` (console failed).
**`backtrace(buf, n)`** stores up to `n` return addresses of the current call stack into `buf` and returns the count.
**`backtrace_symbols(addrs, n)`** returns a single `malloc`ed block holding `n` Text descriptions (`object(symbol+offset) [address]`).
**`backtrace_symbols_fd`** writes the same descriptions to a file descriptor, without allocating.
The first call may load the unwinder (`libgcc_s`) via `dlopen`, so it is not async-signal-safe unless primed.
Frames without unwind information may be omitted.
Symbol names are available only for dynamic symbols.
Provide dynamically sized, suitably aligned blocks of writable memory whose lifetime the caller controls.
**`malloc(n)`** returns a block of at least `n` bytes, aligned for any fundamental type (`alignof(max_align_t)`, 16 on x86_64).
**`calloc(k, n)`** returns a zero-filled block for `k` elements of `n` bytes. If `k*n` overflows `size_t`, it fails with `ENOMEM`.
**`realloc(p, n)`** resizes block `p`, preserving `min(old, n)` bytes. It may move the block.
`realloc(NULL, n)` is `malloc(n)`.
`realloc(p, 0)` frees `p` and returns `NULL` in glibc. ⚑ HIST: implementations disagree (it may return a unique pointer), and C23 made the case undefined.
**`reallocarray(p, k, n)`** is `realloc` with an overflow-checked product.
**`free(p)`** releases a block. `free(NULL)` is a no-op. `free` preserves `errno` (2.33+).
**Aligned forms:**
`aligned_alloc(a, n)` (C11) requires a power-of-two `a`. glibc accepts any `n`; C11 required `n` to be a multiple of `a` until DR 460.
`posix_memalign(&p, a, n)` requires `a` to be a power of two and a multiple of `sizeof(void*)`. It returns the error number directly (`EINVAL`/`ENOMEM`) and leaves `*p` unmodified on failure.
`memalign(a, n)` (obsolete) rounds a non-power-of-two `a` up.
`valloc(n)` returns page-aligned memory.
`pvalloc(n)` returns page-aligned memory with `n` rounded up to a whole page.
**`malloc_usable_size(p)`** returns the number of bytes actually usable in the block, which is at least the requested size.
**`cfree`** is a compat alias for `free`.
Sizes are `size_t`. Requests above `PTRDIFF_MAX` fail with `ENOMEM` (2.29+). The functional reason is that pointer subtraction within an object must be representable.
Distinct live blocks never overlap.
The contents of `malloc` and `realloc` growth are indeterminate. `calloc` contents are zero.
A block's alignment is at least the fundamental alignment, or the requested alignment.
Memory returned is not shared with any other live block, or with library-internal structures.
Failure returns `NULL` with `ENOMEM` (except `posix_memalign`).
`malloc(0)` returns a unique, freeable, non-NULL pointer in glibc. ⚑ ARB: the standard allows either this or NULL.

Double `free`, `free` of a non-heap pointer, and use after free are undefined behaviour. glibc detects many of these and aborts (`free(): invalid pointer`, `double free detected in tcache 2`, `malloc(): corrupted top size`), but does not guarantee to.
A `realloc` failure leaves the original block intact.

MT-Safe. A block may be freed by a different thread than the one that allocated it. Allocation after `fork` in a multi-threaded parent is supported: glibc reinitializes the allocator locks in the child, which is stronger than POSIX requires.

**`mallopt(param, value)`** adjusts allocator policy: `M_MMAP_THRESHOLD`, `M_MMAP_MAX`, `M_TRIM_THRESHOLD`, `M_TOP_PAD`, `M_ARENA_MAX`, `M_ARENA_TEST`, `M_PERTURB`, `M_CHECK_ACTION`, `M_MXFAST`. It returns 1 on success and 0 on error.
**`mallinfo2()`** returns a structure of `size_t` statistics (arena bytes, free chunks, mmapped bytes, in-use bytes, releasable bytes).
**`mallinfo()`** returns the same statistics as `int` fields.
**`malloc_stats()`** prints per-arena statistics to `stderr`.

**`malloc_info(options, fp)`** writes an XML description to `fp`. `options` must be 0; otherwise it fails with `EINVAL`. It returns 0, or -1 with `errno` set (Written 2026-10-04 (owner ruling, phase 12-13 report); malloc_info(3); the reference returns 22).
**`malloc_trim(pad)`** returns free memory to the system, leaving `pad` bytes at the top of the main heap. It returns 1 if any memory was released.

The hook variables are **compat-only** (2.34 removed their effect from `libc.so`). Old binaries can link to them, but they are inert in `libc.so.6`: assigning them does nothing. With `libc_malloc_debug.so` preloaded, only `__malloc_hook`, `__free_hook`, `__realloc_hook`, `__memalign_hook` and `__malloc_initialize_hook` act; `__after_morecore_hook` and `__morecore` stay inert (Written 2026-10-04 (owner ruling, phase 12-13 report), `spec/behaviour/mallocdbg.md`).

**`mcheck(abortfn)`** (with `libc_malloc_debug.so`) enables consistency checking of every block. It must be called before the first allocation. `mprobe(p)` returns the status of one block (`MCHECK_OK`, `MCHECK_HEAD`, `MCHECK_TAIL`, `MCHECK_FREE`, `MCHECK_DISABLED`).
**`mtrace()`** (with `libc_malloc_debug.so`) logs each allocation and free to the file named by `MALLOC_TRACE`. `muntrace()` stops logging.
**`malloc_get_state`/`malloc_set_state`** are compat stubs (Emacs unexec). They now fail.
Allocate `n` bytes in the caller's stack frame. The storage is released when the function returns.
There is no failure indication. Exceeding the stack is undefined, and in practice triggers `SIGSEGV` on the guard page.

A stack-discipline arena. Objects are allocated in order and freed by releasing an object together with everything allocated after it. The arena also supports *growing* an object incrementally before finalizing it.
Chunk-size hint, alignment mask, and caller-supplied chunk allocation and free functions.
Finished objects never move.
A growing object may move until it is finished.
Alignment follows the obstack's alignment mask (default: fundamental alignment).

On allocation failure, `obstack_alloc_failed_handler` is called. Its default prints a message and calls `exit(obstack_exit_failure)`. ⚑ HIST: failure by exiting from inside a library, configured through a global handler.
`brk(addr)` sets the end of the data segment. `sbrk(delta)` moves it by `delta` and returns the old end.
`ENOMEM`.
All functions in this section are pure computations. **Kernel: none.**
All are MT-Safe and AS-Safe, except where stated (`strtok`, `strerror`, locale-dependent collation).
Overlapping source and destination is undefined behaviour unless the entry says otherwise.
⚑ HIST (section-wide). Almost every function here exists in two or more forms whose only difference is *how the extent of an input is delimited*:
byte count (`mem*`);
NUL terminator (`str*`);
NUL terminator *or* a count, whichever comes first (`strn*`);
a destination capacity (`strl*`, `*_chk`).

The functional needs are fewer than 20: copy, move, fill, compare, search for a byte, search for a subsequence, search for any of a set, measure, concatenate, tokenize, duplicate. Each need is multiplied by three to six delimiting conventions, and again by the wide-character (`wcs*`/`wmem*`) versions. ⚑ COMMENTARY: implies that one need gives one answer under every delimiting convention; covered by `s4_n_4`.

A design built on length-delimited **Text** needs one form per need. It needs NUL-terminated forms only at the kernel boundary (Path, argv). ⚑ COMMENTARY: nothing testable (an internal design rule, not observable through the C interface).
Copy a sequence of bytes (or wide characters) from source to destination.
**`memcpy(d, s, n)`** copies `n` bytes. Overlap is undefined. ⚑ COMPAT: `memcpy@GLIBC_2.2.5` tolerates overlap for old binaries; `@GLIBC_2.14` does not.
**`memmove`** copies correctly under overlap.
**`mempcpy`** returns `d + n` instead of `d`.
**`memccpy(d, s, c, n)`** copies up to and including the first byte equal to `c`, at most `n` bytes. It returns a pointer past the copied `c`, or `NULL` if `c` was not found.
**`bcopy(s, d, n)`** is `memmove` with the argument order reversed. ⚑ HIST (BSD); removed from POSIX in 2008.
**`strcpy(d, s)`** copies `s` including its terminator. `stpcpy` returns a pointer to the copied terminator (useful for appending).

**`strncpy(d, s, n)`** copies at most `n` bytes. If `s` is shorter, it pads `d` with zeros to exactly `n` bytes. If `s` is `n` bytes or longer, `d` is **not** terminated. ⚑ HIST: `strncpy` was designed for fixed-width, zero-padded fields (`utmp`, 14-byte directory entries of V7 Unix), not for bounded string copy. It is routinely misused as a bounded copy.
**`stpncpy`** is `strncpy` returning `d + min(strlen(s), n)`.

**`strlcpy(d, s, n)`** (2.38, from BSD) copies at most `n-1` bytes and always terminates if `n > 0`. It returns `strlen(s)`, so a result `≥ n` means truncation. ⚑ HIST: it reads all of `s` even when truncating.
**Wide forms** are the same contracts over `wchar_t` units.
Valid, non-overlapping regions of the stated sizes. For `str*`, the source must be terminated. For `n` variants, `n` may be 0.
On return the destination holds the stated bytes. No other bytes are written, except `strncpy`'s padding.
None reported. A destination overflow is undefined behaviour (C0.5 fortify variants turn it into a controlled abort).
**`memset(d, c, n)`** sets `n` bytes to `(unsigned char)c`.
**`bzero(d, n)`** equals `memset(d, 0, n)`. ⚑ HIST.

**`explicit_bzero(d, n)`** zeroes the bytes, and the zeroing is guaranteed not to be optimized away by the compiler, even when the object is dead afterwards. This is the functional need behind clearing secrets. It is a contract with the compiler, not with the machine: copies in registers or on the stack are not covered.
Establish a total order between two sequences.
**`memcmp`/`strcmp`/`strncmp`** compare lexicographically, treating bytes as `unsigned char`. The result's sign is the order; only the sign is specified.
**`bcmp`** reports only equal or not equal. ⚑ HIST.
**`__memcmpeq`** (2.35) has the equality-only contract of `bcmp`, under a reserved name. It exists so that compilers can emit calls to it when only equality matters.

**`*casecmp`** compare after mapping each byte through the current locale's `tolower`. ⚑ HIST: byte-at-a-time case folding is wrong for multibyte encodings (UTF-8) and for language-specific folding (Turkish dotless i). The functional need, case-insensitive equality of text, requires a Unicode-aware fold, and the interface cannot express one.
**`strcoll`/`wcscoll`** compare according to the collation rules of `LC_COLLATE` (multi-level ISO 14651 ordering). With the "C" locale this is `strcmp`.
**`strverscmp`** (GNU) compares strings that contain embedded decimal numbers, so that "file9" < "file10". It treats leading zeros as fractional parts.

**`_l` variants** take an explicit locale object instead of the thread's current locale. ⚑ PATH: `_l` variants were added throughout the library once per-thread and explicit locales arrived (§7). In a new design an explicit locale (or none) is the base contract.
The comparisons are consistent (a total preorder for a fixed locale). `strcoll` agrees with the ordering of `strxfrm` outputs compared with `strcmp`.
`strcoll` may set `errno` (for example `EINVAL` for invalid multibyte input) and still return a result. ⚑ ARB: there is no sentinel, so detection requires zeroing `errno`.

Transform a string into a key such that `strcmp` on two keys gives the same order as `strcoll` on the originals. Writes at most `n` bytes including the terminator and returns the full key length (excluding the terminator). A result `≥ n` means the output is incomplete, and the contents of the destination are then unspecified.
**`memchr(s, c, n)`** returns the first position in `s[0..n)` holding `(unsigned char)c`, or `NULL`.
**`memrchr`** returns the last such position.
**`rawmemchr(s, c)`** searches without a bound. The caller asserts that `c` occurs.
**`strchr(s, c)`** returns the first occurrence of `c` in the terminated `s`. The terminator itself is searchable: `strchr(s, 0)` returns the end.
**`strchrnul`** returns the end of the string instead of `NULL`.
**`strrchr`** returns the last occurrence.
**`index`/`rindex`** are BSD names for `strchr`/`strrchr`. ⚑ HIST.
Return the first position at which the needle occurs in the haystack, or `NULL`. An empty needle matches at the start. `strcasestr` compares with locale case folding.
Worst-case linear time (a two-way string-matching algorithm). Callers may not rely on this; it is a quality-of-implementation property, not a contract.
**`strspn(s, set)`** returns the length of the longest prefix of `s` consisting only of bytes in `set`.
**`strcspn`** returns the length of the longest prefix consisting only of bytes *not* in `set`.
**`strpbrk`** returns a pointer to the first byte of `s` that is in `set`.
`set` is a Text interpreted as a *set* of bytes. Order and duplicates do not matter, and the byte 0 cannot be a member. ⚑ HIST: a set of bytes delimited by NUL.
`strlen(s)` returns the number of bytes before the terminator. `strnlen(s, n)` returns `min(strlen(s), n)` and reads no more than `n` bytes.
**`strcat(d, s)`** appends `s` to the terminated string in `d`.
**`strncat(d, s, n)`** appends at most `n` bytes of `s`, then a terminator. `n` bounds the *source*, not the destination. ⚑ ARB: this is a frequent source of overflow bugs.
**`strlcat(d, s, size)`** appends while keeping the total length at most `size-1`, and returns `strlen(d_initial) + strlen(s)`. If `d` is not terminated within `size`, it returns `size + strlen(s)`.
Return a new `malloc`ed copy (or, for the `a` forms, a stack copy) of the string, or of at most `n` bytes of it, always terminated.
`NULL` with `ENOMEM`.
Split a mutable string into tokens separated by bytes from a delimiter set.

**`strtok(s, delim)`** skips leading delimiters, terminates the token in place (writes 0), and remembers the position in hidden process-global state. It then returns successive tokens when called with `s == NULL`. Empty tokens are never returned.
**`strtok_r`** keeps the position in a caller variable.
**`strsep(&s, delim)`** (BSD) returns empty tokens, advancing `*s` past the delimiter, and sets `*s = NULL` after the last token.
**`wcstok`** is `strtok_r` for wide strings (ISO C gave it three parameters).
Manage a *list of Text* stored as a single `malloc`ed buffer of concatenated NUL-terminated strings, together with its total length. You can:
create one from an `argv` array or a separator-delimited Text;
count its entries;
convert it back to an `argv`-style pointer array;
join its entries with a separator;
append, insert or delete entries;
iterate over it;
replace substrings in every entry.
Functions return `error_t` (`ENOMEM`), or 0 on success.

Treat an argz vector as a `NAME=VALUE` mapping: look up, add, merge (with or without overriding existing names), remove, and strip null entries. An entry without `=` has a *null* value, which is distinct from an empty value.
Report whether a single-byte character belongs to a class in the current (`LC_CTYPE`) or given locale.

An `int` that must be representable as `unsigned char`, or equal `EOF` (-1). ⚑ HIST, ⚑ ARB: passing a plain `char` holding a negative value (any byte ≥ 0x80 on x86, where `char` is signed) is undefined behaviour. The domain includes `EOF` only so that the result of `getc` can be passed unchecked. The functional need is "classify this byte".
`isctype(c, mask)`/`__isctype` (GNU) test an arbitrary combination of class bits (`_IS*`).

A non-zero result means membership. Class relations hold, for example `isalnum ⇔ isalpha ∨ isdigit`. `isdigit` and `isxdigit` are locale-independent in practice (always `0-9`, `a-f`, `A-F`). `isascii(c)` tests `0 ≤ c ≤ 127`, and `toascii` masks to 7 bits (⚑ HIST, obsolete).

Classify a wide character (a Unicode code point on glibc) according to the locale's character classes. `wctype(name)` looks up a class by name (standard or locale-defined, for example `"jspace"`) and returns an opaque `wctype_t`. `iswctype(wc, t)` tests membership. `WEOF` is a member of no class.
The classes follow the locale's definition, which for glibc's UTF-8 locales is derived from the Unicode Character Database (Unicode 15.1.0 in 2.39).
`wctype` returns 0 for an unknown class.

Map one character to its lower- or uppercase counterpart in the locale. Characters without a counterpart map to themselves. `wctrans(name)` looks up a named mapping (`"tolower"`, `"toupper"`, or locale-defined, for example `"tojhira"`). `towctrans` applies it.

**Kernel: none** for all conversion functions, except `iconv_open`, which loads conversion modules. That needs `openat`, `mmap` and `dlopen` of `gconv` modules, and reads **Config** `gconv-modules` / `gconv-modules.cache` under `GCONV_PATH` or the built-in directory.

The *multibyte encoding* of the locale (`LC_CTYPE` codeset, usually UTF-8) is what these functions convert from and to. On glibc the *wide* representation is always UCS-4 (`__STDC_ISO_10646__` is defined), so `wchar_t` holds exactly one Unicode code point.

An opaque object holding the shift state and partial-character state of an ongoing conversion. A zero-initialized object is the initial state. `mbsinit(ps)` reports whether `ps` is in the initial state (true for `NULL`).
**`mbrtowc(&wc, s, n, ps)`** decodes one character from at most `n` bytes. It returns:
the number of bytes consumed;
0 for the null character;
`(size_t)-2` for an incomplete but valid prefix (all `n` bytes consumed into `ps`);
`(size_t)-1` with `EILSEQ` for an invalid sequence.
**`wcrtomb(s, wc, ps)`** encodes one character into at most `MB_CUR_MAX` bytes and returns the byte count, or `(size_t)-1`/`EILSEQ`.
**`mbrlen`** is `mbrtowc` without storing the result.
**The non-`r` forms (`mblen`, `mbtowc`, `wctomb`)** keep state in hidden static storage. ⚑ HIST, ⚑ PATH: that is why the `r` (restartable) forms exist.
**`btowc(c)`/`wctob(wc)`** convert between a single byte and a wide character when the character is a single byte in the locale encoding. Otherwise they return `WEOF`/`EOF`.
**`mbrtoc16`/`c16rtomb`** convert to and from UTF-16 code units. A character outside the BMP is delivered in two calls:
`mbrtoc16` returns `(size_t)-3` for the second (low) surrogate;
`c16rtomb` buffers a high surrogate in the state.
**`mbrtoc32`/`c32rtomb`** convert to and from UTF-32 code points. **`mbrtoc8`/`c8rtomb`** (2.36, C23) convert to and from UTF-8 code units, one unit per call.

`MB_CUR_MAX` (a runtime value, `__ctype_get_mb_cur_max()`) bounds the bytes per character in the current locale. It is 6 for glibc UTF-8 (a historical maximum), although valid UTF-8 needs at most 4. `MB_LEN_MAX` is the compile-time bound (16).
Output is written only for complete characters.
Invalid or overlong UTF-8, surrogate code points, and values above `0x10FFFF` are rejected with `EILSEQ`.
`s == NULL` resets the state; with an incomplete character pending it is an invalid sequence: `(size_t)-1` with `EILSEQ`.
⚑ HIST: `(size_t)-1`, `-2` and `-3` are in-band sentinel values in an unsigned return type.

Convert a whole terminated string. The `nr` forms limit the *input* length as well as the output. They write at most `len` output units and return the number of units written (excluding the terminator), or `(size_t)-1`/`EILSEQ`. If `dst` is `NULL`, they only measure the output. The `r` forms advance `*src` to the point reached, or set it to `NULL` if the terminator was converted.

**`iconv_open(to, from)`** creates a conversion descriptor between two named encodings. The names are case-insensitive, and aliases are accepted. Suffixes on `to` modify how unconvertible characters are handled:
`//TRANSLIT` approximates them;
`//IGNORE` drops them;
a combined form (2.32+ `//TRANSLIT//IGNORE`) does both.
**`iconv(cd, &in, &inleft, &out, &outleft)`** converts as much input as possible, advancing the pointers and decrementing the counts. It returns the number of *irreversible* conversions performed.
**`iconv(cd, NULL, NULL, &out, &outleft)`** emits the shift sequence that returns the output to the initial state.
**`iconv(cd, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL)`** resets the state.
**`iconv_close`** frees the descriptor.
`iconv_open` returns `(iconv_t)-1` with `EINVAL` if the conversion is unsupported.
`iconv` returns `(size_t)-1` with:
`E2BIG`: output space exhausted;
`EILSEQ`: invalid input, with `*in` left at the invalid sequence;
`EINVAL`: incomplete input at the end.
With `//IGNORE`, `iconv` skips invalid input but still returns -1/`EILSEQ` at the end. ⚑ HIST: this makes "was anything lost?" hard to distinguish from "did it fail?".
The conversion is resumable across calls with no loss. glibc supplies about 1,300 names or aliases for about 200 encodings (the `iconvdata` modules).
Return the number of terminal columns a wide character, or the first `n` characters of a wide string, occupies:
0 for combining and zero-width characters, and for the null character;
2 for East Asian wide and fullwidth characters and most emoji;
1 otherwise;
-1 if any character is non-printable.
A *locale* is a named set of cultural conventions, divided into categories:
| `LC_CTYPE` | character classes, case mapping, multibyte encoding |
| `LC_COLLATE` | string ordering |
| `LC_NUMERIC` | decimal point, thousands grouping (non-monetary) |
| `LC_MONETARY` | currency formatting |
| `LC_TIME` | day and month names, date formats |
| `LC_MESSAGES` | yes/no expressions, message catalog selection |
| `LC_PAPER`, `LC_NAME`, `LC_ADDRESS`, `LC_TELEPHONE`, `LC_MEASUREMENT`, `LC_IDENTIFICATION` | GNU extensions |

Locale-dependent functions consult the thread's current locale. That is the per-thread locale set with `uselocale`, or else the process-global locale set with `setlocale`. `"C"` and `"POSIX"` are built in. `"C.UTF-8"` has been built in since 2.35.
Query or set the global locale for one category or for all categories (`LC_ALL`).
`setlocale(cat, NULL)` returns the current name.
`setlocale(cat, "")` selects the locale from the environment: `LC_ALL`, then `LC_<cat>`, then `LANG`.
The name returned for `LC_ALL` can be passed back to `setlocale` to restore a composite locale.

A category whose current name is the name asked for keeps its data: it is not looked up again, so a changed `LOCPATH` or changed locale files take effect for it only after it has been set to another name (observed).
Returns `NULL` and leaves the locale unchanged if the name is unknown or the data is unavailable.
MT-Unsafe (`const:locale env`). It changes the locale of all threads that have not called `uselocale`. ⚑ HIST.
The returned string is library-owned, and valid until the next `setlocale`.
**`newlocale(mask, name, base)`** creates a locale object with the categories in `mask` taken from `name` and the rest from `base`. `base` is consumed: it may be reused or freed.
**`duplocale`** copies an object.
**`freelocale`** releases an object.
**`uselocale(loc)`** sets the calling thread's locale and returns the previous one. `LC_GLOBAL_LOCALE` reverts to the global locale, and `(locale_t)0` only queries.
`newlocale` returns `(locale_t)0` with `EINVAL` (bad mask) or `ENOENT` (unknown name). ⚑ ARB: freeing a locale that is still in use by a thread is undefined.

**`localeconv()`** returns a `struct lconv` describing the numeric and monetary conventions: `decimal_point`, `thousands_sep`, `grouping`, `int_curr_symbol`, `currency_symbol`, `mon_*`, `positive_sign`, `negative_sign`, `*_frac_digits`, `p_cs_precedes`, and the others.

**`nl_langinfo(item)`** returns one Text item. Items include `CODESET`, `D_T_FMT`, `D_FMT`, `T_FMT`, `DAY_1..7`, `ABDAY_*`, `MON_1..12`, `ABMON_*`, `ALTMON_*` (2.27+), `RADIXCHAR`, `THOUSEP`, `YESEXPR`, `NOEXPR`, `CRNCYSTR`, `ERA`, `ALT_DIGITS`, and GNU items for every category (`_NL_PAPER_HEIGHT`, `_NL_ADDRESS_POSTAL_FMT`, ...).
Pointers are library-owned. They stay valid until the locale changes.

Format one or more `double` or `long double` amounts according to a format string (`%n` national, `%i` international), using `LC_MONETARY`. Flags control fill character, grouping, sign style (`+`, `(`), and the suppression of the currency symbol. It writes at most `max` bytes.
Returns -1 with `E2BIG` if the result does not fit.
Classify a response Text against the locale's `YESEXPR`/`NOEXPR` regular expressions. Returns 1 (yes), 0 (no) or -1 (unrecognized).
Translate a message, identified by its original (msgid) text, into the language of `LC_MESSAGES` (or `LANGUAGE`, a colon-separated preference list).
**`gettext(id)`** returns the translation, or `id` itself if there is none.
**`ngettext(id, id_plural, n)`** selects a plural form using the catalog's plural expression.

**Domains** name separate catalogs. `textdomain` sets the default domain. `bindtextdomain(domain, dir)` sets where catalogs are found (`dir/<lang>/<CATEGORY>/ <domain>.mo`; `<CATEGORY>` is `LC_MESSAGES` except for `dcgettext`/`dcngettext` with another category; corrected 2026-10-04 under the three-way rule: the reference and bindtextdomain(3) agree, `spec/behaviour/catalogs.md`). `bind_textdomain_codeset` sets the output encoding.
`LANGUAGE` is ignored when the `LC_MESSAGES` locale is `C`, `POSIX` or `C.UTF-8`, and a `C` or `POSIX` element in the list ends the search untranslated.

`bindtextdomain` and `bind_textdomain_codeset` with a NULL or empty domain return NULL and leave `errno` unchanged (Written 2026-10-04 (owner ruling, phase 12-13 report), `spec/behaviour/catalogs.md`).
It never fails visibly: failure returns the untranslated text. Returned translations are read-only and library-owned. `errno` is preserved.

Open a catalog by name (searching `NLSPATH` templates with `%N`, `%L`, `%l`, `%t`, `%c` substitutions) and retrieve messages by numeric (set, message) identifiers, returning a default Text if one is missing.

In an `NLSPATH` template, `%t` and `%c` keep the locale name's `@modifier`. The search stops (`EINVAL`) at a candidate that is a directory or not a catalog, rather than trying the remaining templates (Written 2026-10-04 (owner ruling, phase 12-13 report), `spec/behaviour/catalogs.md`).
`catopen` returns `(nl_catd)-1`; an empty name gives `EINVAL`. `catgets` returns the default and sets `errno`.
**Kernel: none** throughout this section.
Locale sensitivity (the radix character, thousands grouping with the GNU `'` flag, and locale digits with `I`) comes from `LC_NUMERIC`.
Parse the longest initial substring of a Text that has the form of an integer in base `b`, and report where parsing stopped.
**The text.** Leading white space (`isspace`) is skipped, and an optional sign is accepted.
**The base** is 2..36, or 0 for automatic detection:
a leading `0` → 8;
`0b`/`0B` → 2 in C23 mode, via the `__isoc23_*` symbols (2.38+);
otherwise 10.
**An optional end pointer** receiving the position after the last consumed character.
On success it returns the value and sets the end pointer.
If no digits are consumed, it returns 0 and the end pointer equals the input.
On overflow it returns `LONG_MAX`/`LONG_MIN`/`ULONG_MAX` (as appropriate) and sets `ERANGE`.

For the unsigned forms a leading `-` is accepted, and the value is negated modulo 2^N. ⚑ HIST, ⚑ ARB: `strtoul("-1")` returns `ULONG_MAX` with no error, which is surprising and not functionally needed.

An invalid base gives `EINVAL`. ⚑ HIST: "no digits" is reported only through the end pointer, and range errors only through `errno`. The caller must zero `errno` and compare pointers. The need is a result that distinguishes {value, no number, out of range}.
Parse the longest initial substring that forms a floating constant, and return the correctly rounded value in the current rounding mode. Accepted forms:
decimal, with an optional exponent (`e`);
hexadecimal (`0x...p±n`);
`INF`/`INFINITY`;
`NAN` and `NAN(n-char-sequence)`, where the payload sets the NaN's mantissa bits. The radix character comes from the locale.
The result is correctly rounded (glibc uses exact arbitrary-precision arithmetic), for any length of input.
Overflow returns `±HUGE_VAL` and sets `ERANGE`.
Underflow returns the correctly rounded subnormal or zero and sets `ERANGE`.
No conversion returns 0 with the end pointer equal to the input.
The same as §8.1 and §8.2, over wide text.

**`strfromd(buf, n, fmt, x)`** (C23/TS 18661) formats `x` using a restricted `printf` conversion: `%[.prec]{a,A,e,E,f,F,g,G}`, with no flags, no width, and no locale grouping. It writes at most `n` bytes and returns the length the full result would have.

**`ecvt(x, ndigit, &decpt, &sign)`** returns `ndigit` significant digits, `ndigit` reduced to a limit the precision gives (17 for `double`, 21 for the `long double` `q` forms). **`fcvt`** returns `ndigit` digits after the point, `ndigit` reduced the same way. Both return the digits only, with the decimal-point position and the sign reported separately.
**`gcvt(x, ndigit, buf)`** formats like `%.*g`.
**The `q` forms** take `long double`.
**The `_r` forms** take a caller buffer.
Digit strings are exact (correctly rounded) representations.
**`abs(n)`** returns |n|. `abs(INT_MIN)` is undefined behaviour. ⚑ ARB: the result type cannot represent it, and C2y adds `uabs` for this.
**`div(n, d)`** returns the quotient (truncated toward zero) and the remainder together. Division by zero, and `INT_MIN / -1`, are undefined.
Pure bit queries on unsigned integers of each standard width. The contracts (for a value of width W bits):
**Counting:** number of leading or trailing zero or one bits. The result is W for 0 when counting zeros.
**Finding:** 1-based index of the first matching bit from the given end, or 0 if none.
**`count_zeros`/`count_ones`:** population counts.
**`has_single_bit`:** true if the value is a power of two.
**`bit_width`:** 1 + floor(log2 x), or 0 for x = 0.
**`bit_floor`:** the largest power of two ≤ x (0 for 0).
**`bit_ceil`:** the smallest power of two ≥ x. The result is 0 if it is not representable. ⚑ ARB, as specified by C23.

Convert between host byte order and big-endian (network) or little-endian order. On x86_64, `hton*` and `ntoh*` are byte swaps. Only `htonl`, `htons`, `ntohl` and `ntohs` are exported functions. The rest are macros.
Return the 1-based index of the least-significant set bit, or 0 if none.
Convert between a `long` (only the low 32 bits are used) and a string of up to 6 characters from `./0-9A-Za-z`, least-significant digit first.
**`getrandom(buf, n, flags)`** fills `buf` with up to `n` bytes from the kernel CSPRNG and returns the count, which may be short for large `n` or when interrupted.
`GRND_NONBLOCK` fails with `EAGAIN` instead of blocking before the pool is initialized.
`GRND_RANDOM` draws from the blocking pool (legacy).
`GRND_INSECURE` (kernel 5.6+) never blocks.

**`getentropy(buf, n)`** fills exactly `n ≤ 256` bytes, or fails with `EIO`. For `n > 256` it fails with `EIO` (POSIX 2024 requires `EINVAL`). ⚑ ARB: the 256-byte limit comes from OpenBSD and is not needed.
**`arc4random()`** returns a uniformly distributed 32-bit value.
**`arc4random_buf(buf, n)`** fills `n` bytes.
**`arc4random_uniform(bound)`** returns a uniform value in `[0, bound)` without modulo bias (0 for bound 0 or 1).
The `arc4random` family never fails and never returns non-random data. If the kernel cannot supply entropy, the process terminates ("cannot get entropy for arc4random").
In glibc 2.39 each call takes its bytes from `getrandom` (there is no user-space buffering), so output is fork-safe.
`getrandom` is a cancellation point. `arc4random` is not.

`rand()` returns a pseudo-random integer in `[0, RAND_MAX]` (`RAND_MAX` = 2^31-1). The sequence is deterministic for a given `srand(seed)`, and the default seed is 1. `rand_r(&seed)` keeps its state in a caller `unsigned int`.
`rand` is MT-Safe in glibc (it takes a lock), although ISO C does not require this.

An additive-feedback generator with caller-selectable state size (8, 32, 64, 128 or 256 bytes). It returns values in `[0, 2^31-1]`. `initstate` supplies a state buffer and returns the previous one. `setstate` switches buffers. The `_r` forms use a caller `struct random_data`.
For a given seed and state size, the sequence is deterministic and identical across glibc versions. Programs depend on this, so the algorithm is effectively a contract.
`initstate` with fewer than 8 bytes returns `NULL`/`EINVAL`.
A 48-bit linear congruential generator
X(n+1) = (a·X(n) + c) mod 2^48, with a = 0x5DEECE66D and c = 0xB.
The algorithm is **part of the contract**: POSIX specifies it exactly, and programs rely on the exact sequence.
`drand48` returns `[0.0, 1.0)`.
`lrand48` returns `[0, 2^31)`.
The `e/n/j` forms take a caller-supplied 3×16-bit state.
`seed48` and `lcong48` set the state and the parameters. `seed48` returns a pointer to a static copy of the previous state.
Each real function `f` exists for every supported floating type, and the name suffix selects the type:
| (none) | `double` | IEEE binary64 |
| `f` | `float` | binary32 |
| `l` | `long double` | x87 80-bit extended |
| `f32` | `_Float32` | binary32 (alias of `f`) |
| `f64` | `_Float64` | binary64 (alias of the unsuffixed form) |
| `f32x` | `_Float32x` | binary64 |
| `f64x` | `_Float64x` | x87 extended (alias of `l`) |
| `f128` | `_Float128` | IEEE binary128 (software) |

The contract is identical across types, apart from the range and precision of the type. This specification documents each function once. ⚑ HIST: C's lack of generic functions produces seven entry points per operation (≈1,000 of the ≈1,150 `libm` symbols). `<tgmath.h>` supplies type-generic macros on top.

`math_errhandling` is `MATH_ERRNO | MATH_ERREXCEPT` on glibc. A domain error sets `EDOM` and raises `FE_INVALID`, and a pole or range error sets `ERANGE` and raises `FE_DIVBYZERO`/`FE_OVERFLOW`/`FE_UNDERFLOW`. A range error sets `ERANGE` when the result overflows to ±∞ or underflows to ±0; a result rounded to the largest finite value (directed rounding) or to a subnormal raises the flags only. Some functions report through the flags only and never set `errno`: `lrint`, `llrint`, `lround`, `llround` (out of range), `fma` and the narrowing `*fma` forms, `remquo`, `logb` (its pole at 0), `nextafter`/`nexttoward` from a zero operand, and the underflow of `erf`. ⚑ HIST: setting `errno` from a pure function defeats vectorization and constant folding, which is why compilers offer `-fno-math-errno`. IEEE exception flags are the functionally sufficient channel. The historical SVID/XPG `matherr` callback and `_LIB_VERSION` selection are compat-only (removed from the API in 2.27).

glibc documents measured maximum ULP errors per function, per type, per architecture (manual "Errors in Math Functions"). It guarantees correct rounding only for the IEEE-required operations: `sqrt`, `fma`, the narrowing arithmetic of §10.4, conversions, `fmod`, `remainder`, and the rounding and classification functions. Other functions are "faithful or better, with documented bounds". A reimplementation must at least match those bounds, because programs (and the glibc test suite's `libm-test-ulps`) depend on them.

The elementary functions of a complex argument with the principal branch cuts of C Annex G. The special cases for infinite and NaN components are specified exhaustively in Annex G, and glibc follows them. `cproj` projects onto the Riemann sphere. `cabs` is `hypot(re, im)`, and `carg` is `atan2(im, re)`.
Query and modify the calling thread's floating-point status (exception flags) and control modes (rounding direction, trap enables):
Clear, raise and test the flags `FE_INVALID`, `FE_DIVBYZERO`, `FE_OVERFLOW`, `FE_UNDERFLOW` and `FE_INEXACT`.
Save and restore the flags as opaque objects (`fexcept_t`).
Get and set the rounding direction: `FE_TONEAREST`, `FE_UPWARD`, `FE_DOWNWARD`, `FE_TOWARDZERO`.
Save and restore the whole environment (`fenv_t`) or only the control modes (`femode_t`).
`feholdexcept` saves the environment, clears the flags, and makes exceptions non-trapping.
`feupdateenv` restores a saved environment and re-raises the saved exceptions.
GNU extensions: `feenableexcept`, `fedisableexcept` and `fegetexcept` control **trapping**, where an exception delivers `SIGFPE`.

They return 0 on success, non-zero on failure. `fesetround` fails for an unsupported mode. Exceptions: `fetestexcept` and `fetestexceptflag` return the set flags, `fegetround` the mode, `feenableexcept` and `fedisableexcept` the previously enabled set (−1 on failure), and `fegetexcept` the enabled set.
Most functions in this section are **thin wrappers**. The contract *is* the kernel's, and glibc adds only:
the errno convention (C0.1);
thread cancellation (C0.2), for blocking calls;
64-bit aliases (C0.4);
occasionally, emulation for older kernels.

Such entries are marked **[thin]**. For them, "Kernel" names the syscall, and the contract is the kernel's documented behaviour (man-pages section 2). Only the caller-visible facts that a reimplementation must preserve are specified here.
⚑ KERN (section-wide): descriptor numbering, open-file-description sharing, the offset model, and the semantics of flags are all kernel ABI.
Resolve a Path, relative to the current directory or to a directory fd (`AT_FDCWD` for the current directory), and return a new fd referring to a new open file description.
**Access mode.** `O_RDONLY`, `O_WRONLY`, `O_RDWR` or `O_PATH`.
**Creation flags.**
`O_CREAT`, `O_EXCL` and `O_TRUNC` create or truncate the file.
`O_NOCTTY` prevents acquiring a controlling terminal, and `O_NOFOLLOW` refuses a final symbolic link. `O_DIRECTORY` requires the Path to be a directory.
`O_CLOEXEC` closes the fd on exec, and `O_TMPFILE` creates an unnamed file.
**Status flags.** `O_APPEND`, `O_NONBLOCK`, `O_SYNC`, `O_DSYNC`, `O_DIRECT`, `O_NOATIME`, `O_ASYNC`, `O_LARGEFILE`.

**Mode.** Required iff `O_CREAT` or `O_TMPFILE`, and passed as a variadic argument. ⚑ HIST: `open` is variadic only because the mode was an optional third argument in V7. The fortify wrapper `__open_2` exists to catch a missing mode at compile time.
The lowest free descriptor number is returned (⚑ KERN).
With `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` the create is atomic, even over most network file systems.
The mode is masked by `umask`, or by the directory's default ACL.
`creat(p, m)` = `open(p, O_CREAT|O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC, m)`. ⚑ HIST.

The kernel's errors: `EACCES`, `EEXIST`, `ENOENT`, `ENOTDIR`, `ELOOP`, `EMFILE` (per-process limit, `RLIMIT_NOFILE`), `ENFILE`, `ENAMETOOLONG`, `EISDIR`, `EROFS`, `ETXTBSY`, `EOVERFLOW`, `EINTR` (FIFOs, or blocking opens of devices), and others.
Yes.

Release a descriptor. The underlying open file description is released when its last descriptor closes. `close_range(lo, hi, flags)` closes (or, with `CLOSE_RANGE_CLOEXEC`, marks close-on-exec) every descriptor in `[lo, hi]`. `closefrom(lo)` closes all descriptors ≥ lo and never fails.
After `close` returns, even with `EINTR` or `EIO`, the descriptor is released. It must **not** be closed again, since the number may already have been reused.
`EBADF`, `EINTR`, `EIO` (for example, deferred write errors on NFS).

**`read(fd, buf, n)`** transfers up to `n` bytes from the file at the description's offset (or from the stream, for pipes, sockets and ttys) into `buf`, and advances the offset. It returns the count, which may be short: at end of file, for pipes and ttys, on signal interruption after partial transfer, and at the per-call cap. It returns 0 at end of file.
**`write`** transfers up to `n` bytes from `buf`. It may be short (full device, pipe capacity, signal, `RLIMIT_FSIZE`).
**`pread`/`pwrite`** use an explicit offset and do not move the file offset. ⚑ KERN: `pwrite` on an `O_APPEND` descriptor appends regardless of the offset (a Linux deviation from POSIX).

**The `v` forms** perform scatter/gather across an array of `(base, len)` pairs, of at most `IOV_MAX` = 1024 entries. The transfer is atomic with respect to other writers on the same description, as for a single write.
**The `v2` forms** add per-call flags: `RWF_HIPRI`, `RWF_DSYNC`, `RWF_SYNC`, `RWF_NOWAIT`, `RWF_APPEND`. An offset of -1 means "use the current offset".
`n` up to `SSIZE_MAX`. ⚑ KERN: Linux transfers at most 0x7ffff000 bytes per call, so callers must loop.
Writes to a pipe of at most `PIPE_BUF` (4096) bytes are atomic.
On success the byte count is exact. A regular-file `write` that returns `n` has updated the page cache. Durability requires §11.8.
`EAGAIN`/`EWOULDBLOCK` for non-blocking I/O.
`EINTR` if interrupted before any transfer.
`EPIPE` plus `SIGPIPE` for a broken pipe or socket.
`EFBIG`, `ENOSPC`, `EDQUOT`, `EIO`, `EISDIR`, `EINVAL` (bad alignment for `O_DIRECT`), `EBADF`, `EFAULT`, `EOVERFLOW`.
Yes.

Set the description's offset relative to the start (`SEEK_SET`), the current position (`SEEK_CUR`) or the end (`SEEK_END`). Also find the next data or hole region (`SEEK_DATA`/`SEEK_HOLE`). Returns the resulting offset.
`ESPIPE` on pipes, sockets and FIFOs.
`EINVAL` for a negative result or a bad `whence`.
`ENXIO` for `SEEK_DATA`/`SEEK_HOLE` beyond the end of file.
`EOVERFLOW`.
**`dup(fd)`** returns the lowest free descriptor, sharing the description.
**`dup2(old, new)`** makes `new` refer to `old`'s description, closing `new` first (atomically). If `old == new`, it validates `old` and returns it.
**`dup3`** is like `dup2`, but accepts `O_CLOEXEC` and fails with `EINVAL` if `old == new`.
**`fcntl(fd, cmd, ...)`** has these commands:
duplication: `F_DUPFD`, `F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC`;
descriptor flags: `F_GETFD`/`F_SETFD` (`FD_CLOEXEC`);
status flags: `F_GETFL`/`F_SETFL`;
locks: `F_GETLK`, `F_SETLK`, `F_SETLKW`, and the open-file-description locks `F_OFD_GETLK`, `F_OFD_SETLK`, `F_OFD_SETLKW`;
signal-driven I/O: `F_GETOWN`, `F_SETOWN`, `F_GETOWN_EX`, `F_SETOWN_EX`, `F_GETSIG`, `F_SETSIG`;
leases and notification: `F_SETLEASE`, `F_GETLEASE`, `F_NOTIFY`;
pipe size: `F_GETPIPE_SZ`, `F_SETPIPE_SZ`;
file seals: `F_ADD_SEALS`, `F_GET_SEALS`;
write-lifetime hints: `F_GET_RW_HINT`, `F_SET_RW_HINT`, `F_GET_FILE_RW_HINT`, `F_SET_FILE_RW_HINT`.
**`getdtablesize()`** returns the `RLIMIT_NOFILE` soft limit. ⚑ HIST.
Perform a device- or file-system-specific operation identified by a request number, with one untyped argument.
Wait until one or more descriptors are ready (readable, writable, exceptional, hang-up), until a timeout expires, or until a signal arrives.
**`select`** uses three fixed-size bit sets, rewrites them on return, and takes a `struct timeval` timeout that Linux updates with the remaining time.
**`pselect`** takes a `timespec` and atomically swaps the signal mask for the duration of the wait.
**`poll`** takes an array of `{fd, events, revents}` and a millisecond timeout. **`ppoll`** takes a `timespec` and a signal mask.
**epoll** is a kernel-held interest set:
`epoll_ctl` adds, modifies or deletes entries with edge- or level-triggered, `EPOLLONESHOT`, `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` and `EPOLLWAKEUP` semantics;
`epoll_wait` returns ready entries with the caller's 64-bit cookie;
`epoll_pwait2` takes a `timespec`.
`epoll_create(size)` ignores `size` (it must be > 0). ⚑ HIST.

For `select`, descriptors must be `< FD_SETSIZE` (1024). ⚑ ARB, ⚑ HIST: `fd_set` is a fixed 1024-bit array baked into the ABI, and a larger descriptor overflows it (fortify `__fdelt_chk` aborts). This is the main reason `select` is unusable in large programs. `poll` and epoll have no such limit.
They return the number of ready descriptors, or 0 on timeout. A negative `fd` in `poll` is ignored.
`EINTR`, `EBADF`, `EINVAL` (nfds > `RLIMIT_NOFILE`), `ENOMEM`.
Yes.
**`fsync(fd)`** does not return until the file's data and metadata are on stable storage. **`fdatasync`** omits metadata that is not needed to retrieve the data.
**`sync()`** schedules a flush of all file systems. On Linux it waits. **`syncfs(fd)`** flushes one file system.
**`sync_file_range(fd, off, n, flags)`** controls writeback of a range. It gives **no** durability guarantee for metadata.
**`posix_fadvise(fd, off, len, advice)`** declares the access pattern: `NORMAL`, `SEQUENTIAL`, `RANDOM`, `WILLNEED`, `DONTNEED`, `NOREUSE`. It returns the error number directly (C0.1).
**`readahead`** is a Linux-specific prefetch.

**`posix_fallocate`** guarantees that the space for the range is allocated, and extends the file if needed. It returns the error number directly. If the file system lacks `fallocate`, glibc **emulates** it by writing a byte into every block. ⚑ HIST: this emulation is slow, racy with concurrent writers, and cannot work on `O_APPEND` descriptors.
**`fallocate(fd, mode, off, len)`** is the Linux call with modes such as `FALLOC_FL_PUNCH_HOLE`, `FALLOC_FL_COLLAPSE_RANGE`, `FALLOC_FL_ZERO_RANGE` and `FALLOC_FL_KEEP_SIZE`. It has no emulation.
**`ftruncate`/`truncate`** set the file length. Extension reads as zeros.
Move data between descriptors without copying it through user memory.
**`sendfile(out, in, &off, n)`**: `in` must be mmap-able. Since Linux 2.6.33, `out` may be any file.
**`copy_file_range`** works between regular files, possibly as a reflink or a server-side copy.
**`splice`** works when one end is a pipe. **`tee`** duplicates pipe contents. **`vmsplice`** maps user pages into a pipe.
Returns the count transferred, which may be short.
`EINVAL` or `EXDEV` for unsupported combinations. Callers must then fall back to `read`/`write`. ⚑ HIST: glibc does not emulate `copy_file_range` (it did briefly, then removed the emulation in 2.30).
**`mmap(addr, len, prot, flags, fd, off)`** creates a mapping of a file (`MAP_SHARED`, `MAP_PRIVATE`, `MAP_SHARED_VALIDATE`) or of anonymous memory (`MAP_ANONYMOUS`). Other flags:
placement: `MAP_FIXED`, `MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE`;
population and residency: `MAP_POPULATE`, `MAP_LOCKED`, `MAP_NORESERVE`;
huge pages: `MAP_HUGETLB` with a size encoding;
stacks: `MAP_GROWSDOWN`, `MAP_STACK`;

**`madvise`** gives usage advice with Linux semantics. `MADV_DONTNEED` *discards* anonymous contents (a semantic effect, not advice). ⚑ HIST: advice with side effects.
**`posix_madvise`** is the POSIX subset. It never discards data: glibc maps `POSIX_MADV_DONTNEED` to a no-op for that reason. It returns the error number directly.
**`process_madvise`/`process_mrelease`** apply advice to, or reap, another process's memory through a pidfd.
**`mremap`** grows, shrinks or moves a mapping. It is variadic, with a new-address argument for `MREMAP_FIXED`.
**`remap_file_pages`** is deprecated and kernel-emulated.
**`msync`** flushes a shared mapping (`MS_SYNC`, `MS_ASYNC`, `MS_INVALIDATE`). It is a cancellation point.
**`mincore`** reports the residency of each page.
**`mlock`, `mlock2` (`MLOCK_ONFAULT`), `munlock`, `mlockall(MCL_CURRENT|MCL_FUTURE| MCL_ONFAULT)`, `munlockall`** pin pages in RAM.
