`NULL` on failure. The `_r` forms return an errno value, where `ERANGE` means "buffer too small".
Enumerate or look up entries of the NSS `aliases` database (`struct aliasent`: name, members, local flag).

Return the calling process's real, effective and saved user and group IDs, and its supplementary group list. `getgroups(0, NULL)` returns the count. `group_member(g)` (GNU) tests whether `g` is the effective GID or a supplementary group.
These calls never fail, except `getgroups` with `EINVAL` when the buffer is too small.
Change the process's user or group identities, following the POSIX rules:
A privileged process (one with `CAP_SETUID`/`CAP_SETGID`) may set any values.
An unprivileged process may only switch among its real, effective and saved IDs.
`setuid` with privilege sets all three. Also:
**`setgroups`** replaces the supplementary list. It requires privilege, and is denied in a user namespace when `/proc/self/setgroups` is `deny`.
**`initgroups(user, g)`** sets the supplementary list to all groups that `user` belongs to, plus `g`.
**`setfsuid`/`setfsgid`** set the file-system IDs used for access checks. They return the previous value and *cannot report failure*. ⚑ HIST.
**The change applies to every thread in the process atomically**, as POSIX requires.
`EPERM`, `EINVAL`, `EAGAIN` (`RLIMIT_NPROC` on some kernels).
**Look up a user record** (`struct passwd`: name, password placeholder, UID, GID, GECOS, home directory, shell) by name or by UID. Or enumerate all records, reading from NSS.
**Look up a group record** (`struct group`: name, password, GID, member-name list) in the same way.
**The `f` forms** parse records from a caller-supplied stream in `/etc/passwd` format. **`putpwent`/`putgrent`** write one.
**`getgrouplist(user, g, groups, &n)`** lists the GIDs of all groups the user belongs to. If the array is too small, it returns -1 and sets `*n` to the needed size.
**`getpw(uid, buf)`** writes a passwd line into an unbounded buffer. ⚑ HIST.
Results come from NSS (§16.1). The non-`_r` forms return static storage (⚑ PATH: hence the `_r` forms).

**Non-`_r` forms** return `NULL`. "Not found" is *not* an error: `errno` is left unchanged, or set to 0, `ENOENT`, `ESRCH`, `EBADF` or `EPERM` depending on the source. ⚑ HIST: POSIX allows several values here, so "not found" and "failed" are hard to tell apart.

**`_r` forms** return 0 with `*result == NULL` for not found, or an errno value (`ERANGE` means the caller buffer is too small; `sysconf(_SC_GETPW_R_SIZE_MAX)` gives only a hint). ⚑ HIST: the "guess a buffer size, retry on ERANGE" protocol.
**End of an enumeration** (`getpwent`, `getgrent`, `getspent`, `getsgent`): the non-`_r` forms return `NULL` with `errno` unchanged; the `_r` forms return `ENOENT`, `errno` unchanged.

The same pattern as §17.3, for `struct spwd` (the password hash and aging fields: last change, min, max, warn, inactive, expire) and `struct sgrp` (the group password, admins and members). The `s` forms parse one Text line.

**`getlogin()`** returns the name of the user logged in on the process's controlling session. glibc reads `/proc/self/loginuid` and maps it through the passwd database. If the audit login UID is unset, it falls back to the `utmp` entry for the controlling terminal.
**`ttyslot()`** returns the index of the current terminal's entry in the terminal table. ⚑ HIST.

**`getpass(prompt)`** opens `/dev/tty` (or uses stdin and stderr), disables echo, reads one line into a static buffer, and restores the terminal. ⚑ HIST: it is obsolete and the buffer is static. glibc puts no limit on the line's length (getpass(3), NOTES).
`getlogin` returns `NULL` with `ENXIO` or `ENOENT` when there is no login session.

Enumerate the shells listed in `/etc/shells`. If the file is absent, the list is `/bin/sh` and `/bin/csh`. Programs such as `chsh` and `ftpd` use it to decide whether a user has a "real" shell. The cursor is process-global.
Read and write the login records database:
`utmp`: current sessions, in `/var/run/utmp`;
`wtmp`: login and logout history, in `/var/log/wtmp`;

`btmp`: failed logins. The records are `struct utmp`/`utmpx`: type (`USER_PROCESS`, `DEAD_PROCESS`, `LOGIN_PROCESS`, `BOOT_TIME`, ...), PID, line, ID, user, host, exit status, session, time and address.
**`getutid`/`getutline`** search by type and ID, or by line. **`pututline`** writes the record, replacing the matching one.
**`login`/`logout`/`logwtmp`** (BSD, from `libutil`) are convenience wrappers.
**`utmpname`** selects a different file.
Record updates are serialized with `fcntl` locks, with a 10-second timeout (⚑ ARB).
Return the calling process's ID (its thread-group ID), its parent's ID, or the calling thread's kernel ID. These calls never fail.

**`fork()`** creates a child process that is a copy of the caller. Copied: memory (copy-on-write), descriptors (sharing descriptions), the signal mask and dispositions, the cwd, the umask, limits, and so on. Returns: 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent.
Only the calling thread exists in the child.
`pthread_atfork` handlers run: *prepare* in reverse registration order before the fork, and *parent* and *child* in registration order after it.
glibc makes its own internal state (malloc, stdio lists, dynamic-linker locks) consistent in the child.
**`_Fork()`** (2.34, POSIX 2024) forks without running `atfork` handlers and without internal lock handling. It is async-signal-safe.

**`vfork()`** creates a child that shares the parent's memory. The parent is suspended until the child calls `execve` or `_exit`. The child may do nothing else. ⚑ HIST: `vfork` is an optimization that predates copy-on-write, and it is dangerous to use correctly. `posix_spawn` is the safe interface to the same primitive.

**`clone(fn, stack, flags, arg, [ptid, tls, ctid])`** is the Linux primitive. It creates a task that shares selected resources (`CLONE_VM`, `CLONE_FS`, `CLONE_FILES`, `CLONE_SIGHAND`, `CLONE_THREAD`, the namespaces, `CLONE_PIDFD`, `CLONE_SETTLS`, ...) and runs `fn(arg)` on the given stack. The child's return value from `fn` is its exit status. There is no public `clone3` wrapper in 2.39.
-1 with `EAGAIN` (`RLIMIT_NPROC`, or the kernel limit) or `ENOMEM`.
The child may call only async-signal-safe functions until it calls `exec`, per POSIX. glibc goes further: `malloc` works in the child.

Replace the process image with a new program, with the argument list and environment given. The PID, descriptors not marked close-on-exec, the signal mask, ignored signals (caught ones are reset to default), the cwd, limits and credentials are all preserved. Set-user-ID and file capabilities are applied.

**The `p` forms** search `$PATH` (the default is `/bin:/usr/bin`) for a name without `/`. If the file exists but is not a valid executable (`ENOEXEC`), they run it with `/bin/sh`. They continue past `EACCES` and report `EACCES` only if no later entry succeeds.
**The `l` forms** take a variadic, NULL-terminated argument list.
**The `e` forms** take an explicit environment. The other forms use `environ`.
**`fexecve(fd, ...)`** executes an open file, via `execveat(fd, "", AT_EMPTY_PATH)`, or `/proc/self/fd/N` on older kernels.
**`execveat`** (2.34) is a thin wrapper.
They do not return on success.
`E2BIG` (argv plus envp exceed the kernel limit, a quarter of `RLIMIT_STACK`, or `MAX_ARG_STRLEN` = 32 pages per string), `EACCES`, `ENOENT`, `ENOEXEC`, `ETXTBSY`, `ENOMEM`, `ELOOP`, `EPERM`.
Create a child process running a new program, applying a list of descriptor actions and attributes in the child before `exec`, and report the child's PID (or, for `pidfd_spawn`, a pidfd).
**File actions**, applied in order: open, close, dup2 (with `fd == newfd`, it clears `FD_CLOEXEC`), chdir, fchdir, closefrom, and tcsetpgrp.
**Attribute flags:**
`POSIX_SPAWN_RESETIDS`: use the real IDs;
`POSIX_SPAWN_SETPGROUP`, `POSIX_SPAWN_SETSID`;
`POSIX_SPAWN_SETSIGMASK`, `POSIX_SPAWN_SETSIGDEF`: reset listed signals to default;
`POSIX_SPAWN_SETSCHEDULER`, `POSIX_SPAWN_SETSCHEDPARAM`;
`POSIX_SPAWN_USEVFORK` (ignored);
`POSIX_SPAWN_SETCGROUP` (2.39, Linux 5.7+).

Returns 0 on success, or an error number. **Errors that occur in the child before `exec` succeeds are reported to the parent as the return value**, not as a child exit status. glibc has guaranteed this since 2.24.
Signal handlers do not run in the child between clone and exec: all signals are blocked, and caught signals are reset.
It is safe in multi-threaded programs.
The error numbers of the failing action, `fork` or `exec`.
**`pidfd_open(pid, flags)`** returns a descriptor that refers stably to a process. It becomes readable (for `poll`) when the process exits. `flags` may be `PIDFD_NONBLOCK`.
**`pidfd_getfd(pidfd, targetfd, 0)`** duplicates a descriptor out of another process.
**`pidfd_send_signal`** sends a signal without PID-reuse races.
**`pidfd_getpid(pidfd)`** (2.39) returns the PID, parsed from `/proc/self/fdinfo/N`.
`ESRCH` (the process is gone), `EPERM`, `EINVAL`.
Wait for a state change of a child and collect its status.
The state changes are: exited, killed by a signal, stopped, or continued (`WUNTRACED`, `WCONTINUED`).
**`waitpid(pid, &status, options)`** selects by PID, process group (`-pgid` or 0), or any child (-1).

**`waitid(idtype, id, &info, options)`** returns a `siginfo_t` with the full status. `idtype` may be `P_PID`, `P_PGID`, `P_ALL` or `P_PIDFD`, and options include `WEXITED`, `WSTOPPED`, `WCONTINUED` and `WNOWAIT`.
**`wait3`/`wait4`** also return the child's resource usage.
Status macros decode the value: `WEXITSTATUS` gives the 8-bit exit code, `WTERMSIG` the signal, and `WCOREDUMP`, `WSTOPSIG` and `WIFCONTINUED` the rest. A reaped child no longer exists as a zombie.
`ECHILD` (no matching children, or `SIGCHLD` is ignored so children are auto-reaped), `EINTR`, `EINVAL`.
Yes.

**`system(cmd)`** runs `/bin/sh -c cmd`. While it waits, it blocks `SIGCHLD` and ignores `SIGINT` and `SIGQUIT` in the caller. It returns the wait status, or -1 on failure. If the shell could not be executed, the status is exit code 127. `system(NULL)` reports whether a shell is available.
**`popen(cmd, "r"|"w"|"re"|"we")`** runs the command with a pipe connected to its stdout or stdin, and returns a stream. **`pclose`** closes the stream, waits for the child, and returns its status.
`system` is MT-Safe in 2.39. Concurrent calls share the `SIGINT` and `SIGQUIT` disposition changes, which are reference-counted.
**`setpgid(pid, pgid)`** moves a process into a new or existing group in the same session.
**`setsid()`** creates a new session and group with the caller as leader, with no controlling terminal. It fails with `EPERM` if the caller is already a group leader.
**`getsid`, `getpgid` and `getpgrp`** query.
**`setpgrp()`** is `setpgid(0, 0)`. ⚑ HIST: the SVID and BSD versions differ, and `__bsd_getpgrp` is the compat symbol for the BSD form.

**`daemon(nochdir, noclose)`** forks and the parent exits. The child calls `setsid`, changes to `/` unless `nochdir`, and redirects 0–2 to `/dev/null` unless `noclose`. It does **not** fork a second time, so the daemon may reacquire a controlling terminal. ⚑ HIST.

**`prctl(option, ...)`** gets or sets per-process or per-thread attributes: name, dumpable, no-new-privs, seccomp, parent-death signal, child subreaper, capability bounding set, memory tagging, and so on. It is variadic.
**`personality(p)`** sets the execution domain flags (for example `ADDR_NO_RANDOMIZE`).
**`unshare(flags)`** detaches the caller from shared namespaces or resources. **`setns(fd, nstype)`** joins a namespace.
**`arch_prctl(code, addr)`** gets or sets x86 architecture state (FS and GS base, CPUID faulting, AMX permissions). ⚑ KERN.
**`ptrace(request, pid, addr, data)`** traces a process. The variadic glibc prototype returns the peeked word for `PEEK*` requests, so a caller must zero `errno` to detect errors. ⚑ HIST.
**`tcgetattr`/`tcsetattr`** read and write a terminal's line-discipline settings (`struct termios`):
input, output, control and local mode flags;
control characters (`VINTR`, `VEOF`, `VMIN`, `VTIME`, ...);
line speeds. `tcsetattr` applies the settings immediately (`TCSANOW`), after output drains (`TCSADRAIN`), or after draining and flushing input (`TCSAFLUSH`).
**The `cf*` functions** get and set speeds as `B*` constants.
**`cfmakeraw`** configures raw mode.
**`tcsendbreak`** sends a break. **`tcdrain`** waits for output to drain (a cancellation point). **`tcflush`** discards queued data. **`tcflow`** suspends or resumes output or input.
**`tcgetsid`** returns the session that owns the terminal.
**`isatty(fd)`** reports whether `fd` is a terminal (`ENOTTY` otherwise).
`ENOTTY`, `EINVAL`, `EINTR`, `EIO` (background process group, orphaned).
**`tcgetpgrp(fd)`** returns the foreground process group of the terminal.
**`tcsetpgrp(fd, pgrp)`** makes `pgrp` the foreground group. When a background process calls it, it sends `SIGTTOU` unless that signal is blocked or ignored.
Return the Path of the terminal device open on `fd`. The non-`_r` form uses a static buffer (⚑ PATH).
`ENOTTY`: `fd` is not a terminal.
`ENODEV`: the device exists, but not in this mount namespace's `/dev`, for example inside a container with a different `/dev/pts`.
`ERANGE`: the buffer is too small.
**`posix_openpt(flags)`** opens a new master side (`O_RDWR`, `O_NOCTTY`).
**`grantpt(fd)`** sets ownership and permissions of the slave. On Linux with devpts this is already done by the kernel, so glibc only validates `fd`.
**`unlockpt(fd)`** unlocks the slave so it can be opened.
**`ptsname(fd)`** returns the slave's Path. It uses static storage (⚑ PATH).
**`openpty(&master, &slave, name, termp, winp)`** creates a pair, opening both sides and optionally applying attributes and a window size.
**`forkpty`** does `openpty` + `fork` + `login_tty` in the child.
**`login_tty(fd)`** makes `fd` the controlling terminal of a new session and redirects descriptors 0–2 to it.
`EAGAIN`/`ENOENT` (no ptys available), `EINVAL`/`ENOTTY` (not a master).
`getttyent` and the related functions read `/etc/ttys` (BSD). `gtty`, `stty` and `revoke` are compat stubs that fail with `ENOSYS`. ⚑ COMPAT.
A *signal* is an asynchronous notification identified by a number from 1 to 64 (`_NSIG` = 65 on Linux):
standard signals 1–31;

real-time signals `SIGRTMIN`..`SIGRTMAX`, which are 34–64 as visible to applications. Each signal has, per process, a *disposition*: default, ignore, or a handler. Each thread has a *mask* of blocked signals. Signals are either pending per thread or pending per process. Standard signals do not queue: a second pending instance is merged. Real-time signals queue, carry a value, and are delivered lowest-numbered first.
**`sigaction(sig, &act, &old)`** sets and gets the disposition. `act` holds the handler (or `SIG_DFL`/`SIG_IGN`), a mask added during the handler, and flags:
`SA_SIGINFO`: a three-argument handler receiving `siginfo_t` and `ucontext_t`;
`SA_RESTART`: C0.3;
`SA_NODEFER`, `SA_RESETHAND`;
`SA_ONSTACK`: use the alternate stack;
`SA_NOCLDSTOP`, `SA_NOCLDWAIT`: child-related behaviour.

**`signal(sig, handler)`** in glibc has **BSD semantics**: the handler stays installed, the signal is blocked during the handler, and calls restart. `sysv_signal` gives the SVR4 semantics: one-shot handler, no blocking, no restart. ⚑ HIST: the meaning of `signal` differs between Unix families. ISO C left it unspecified, which makes `signal` unportable.
**`siginterrupt(sig, flag)`** toggles `SA_RESTART`.
**`sigset`, `sighold`, `sigrelse`, `sigignore`** are SVR4 forms (removed from POSIX in 2024). ⚑ HIST.
**`ssignal`/`gsignal`** are SVID software signals (`gsignal` = `raise`). ⚑ HIST.
**`sigvec`** is 4.2BSD, compat only.
**`sigreturn`** is an exported stub that always fails with `ENOSYS`. The real return from a handler goes through the restorer described below.
`EINVAL`: an invalid signal, an attempt to catch or ignore `SIGKILL` or `SIGSTOP`, or a glibc-internal signal.

**`pthread_sigmask(how, &set, &old)`** changes the calling thread's mask with `SIG_BLOCK`, `SIG_UNBLOCK` or `SIG_SETMASK`. It returns an error number. **`sigprocmask`** is the same with the `errno` convention.
**The set operations** manipulate a `sigset_t`. `sigisemptyset`, `sigandset` and `sigorset` are GNU. The `__sig*` forms are inline helpers.
**`sigblock`, `sigsetmask` and `siggetmask`** are BSD forms that use an `int` mask of the first 31 signals. ⚑ HIST.
**`sigpause`** has two contracts selected by feature macros: BSD takes a mask, and XSI (`__xpg_sigpause`) takes a signal to remove from the mask. ⚑ HIST.
`SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` cannot be blocked, and are silently removed from the set. So are glibc's internal signals.
**`kill(pid, sig)`** sends to a process. `pid` 0 means the caller's group, -1 means all processes the caller may signal, and `-pgid` means a group. `sig` 0 only checks existence and permission.
**`killpg(pgrp, sig)`** sends to a group.
**`raise(sig)`** sends to the calling thread. The signal is delivered before `raise` returns, if unblocked.
**`sigqueue(pid, sig, value)`** sends with an attached `sigval`. It queues, for real-time signals.
**`pthread_kill(thread, sig)`** targets a thread in this process. **`pthread_sigqueue`** (GNU) does the same with a value.
**`tgkill(tgid, tid, sig)`** (2.30) is a thin wrapper.
`EINVAL`, `EPERM`, `ESRCH`. `pthread_kill` on a thread that has exited but not been joined returns 0 in 2.34+.
**`pause()`** sleeps until a handler runs, then returns -1/`EINTR`.
**`sigsuspend(&mask)`** atomically replaces the mask and waits for a handler to run, then restores the mask.
**`sigwait(&set, &sig)`** synchronously accepts a pending signal from `set`, which should be blocked. It returns the signal number through `sig`, and an error number as its result.
**`sigwaitinfo`/`sigtimedwait`** do the same with `siginfo_t` and an optional timeout (`EAGAIN` on timeout).
**`sigpending(&set)`** reports the pending signals.
All the waiting functions are cancellation points.
Create or modify a descriptor that returns pending signals from a mask as `struct signalfd_siginfo` records when read. The signals must be blocked in order to be received this way.
Define a per-thread memory region on which handlers flagged `SA_ONSTACK` run. This allows handling stack overflow. `SS_DISABLE` disables it, and `SS_AUTODISARM` (kernel 4.7+) disarms it while in use.

The size must be at least `MINSIGSTKSZ`. ⚑ KERN, ⚑ HIST: since 2.34, `MINSIGSTKSZ` and `SIGSTKSZ` are **not constants** under `_DYNAMIC_STACK_SIZE_SOURCE`/ `_GNU_SOURCE`. They call `sysconf(_SC_MINSIGSTKSZ)`, because AVX-512 and AMX signal frames exceed the historical 2 KiB/8 KiB constants. The kernel reports the real minimum in `AT_MINSIGSTKSZ`.
**`strsignal(sig)`** returns a translated description. The storage is per-thread for unknown signals.
**`sigdescr_np`** returns the untranslated description, and **`sigabbrev_np`** returns the name without `SIG` (for example `"INT"`). Both were added in 2.32.
**`psignal(sig, s)`** and **`psiginfo(info, s)`** print to `stderr`.

A handler runs on the interrupted thread, with the signal (and `sa_mask`) blocked. It may call only async-signal-safe functions, per the POSIX list: `write`, `read`, `_exit`, `sigaction`, `kill`, `raise`, `open`, `close`, `fork`/`_Fork`, `execve`, `waitpid`, `sem_post`, `clock_gettime`, and others. It must save and restore `errno`. Returning from a handler for a synchronous fault (`SIGSEGV`, `SIGBUS`, `SIGFPE`, `SIGILL`) that does not fix the cause re-executes the faulting instruction.
**`setjmp(env)`** saves the calling environment (callee-saved registers, stack pointer, program counter, and for `sigsetjmp(env, 1)` the signal mask). It returns 0 when called directly.
**`longjmp(env, v)`** restores the environment so that `setjmp` appears to return `v` (1 if `v` is 0). The function that called `setjmp` must not have returned.
**`_setjmp`/`_longjmp`** never save or restore the mask. **`setjmp`** on glibc does not save the mask either (BSD would). ⚑ HIST: the default differs by Unix family.

**`__longjmp_chk`** is the fortified form. It aborts if the jump would move to a frame *below* the current stack pointer (an invalid jump), except for jumps between the alternate signal stack and the main stack.

`setjmp` may appear only in restricted syntactic contexts (as a whole expression statement, or in a comparison inside `if`/`while`/`switch`). Local non-`volatile` variables modified after `setjmp` have indeterminate values after `longjmp`. ⚑ HIST: `setjmp` is a function that "returns twice", which compilers must special-case.
On x86_64 the saved stack and return addresses are mangled with a per-process secret (pointer guard). With CET, the shadow stack is unwound to match (via `incssp`).
**`getcontext(&uc)`** saves the full user context (registers, signal mask, stack description).
**`setcontext(&uc)`** resumes it.

**`makecontext(&uc, fn, argc, ...)`** modifies a context so that resuming it calls `fn` with `argc` integer arguments on the stack in `uc.uc_stack`. When `fn` returns, it resumes `uc.uc_link`, or exits the thread if that is NULL.
**`swapcontext(&old, &new)`** saves into `old` and resumes `new`.
Arguments to `makecontext` must be `int`-sized. ⚑ HIST: on 64-bit ABIs, passing pointers is technically non-portable, although glibc supports 64-bit values on x86_64.
Since 2.34 all of `libpthread` is in `libc.so.6`. `libpthread.so.0` remains as an empty placeholder (⚑ COMPAT).
Pthread functions return **error numbers** and do not set `errno` (C0.1). The exceptions are `sem_*`, which use `errno`.

**Kernel (section-wide).** Thread synchronization rests on one primitive, the **futex** (`futex`/`futex_time64`), with operations `FUTEX_WAIT`, `FUTEX_WAKE`, `FUTEX_WAIT_BITSET` (absolute timeouts on a chosen clock), `FUTEX_LOCK_PI`, `FUTEX_UNLOCK_PI`, `FUTEX_TRYLOCK_PI`, `FUTEX_LOCK_PI2`, `FUTEX_CMP_REQUEUE_PI` and `FUTEX_WAIT_REQUEUE_PI`. The uncontended paths are pure user-space atomic instructions. The futex syscall itself is not exported by glibc; callers use `syscall()`.

**`pthread_create(&t, attr, fn, arg)`** starts a new thread in the process running `fn(arg)`. The new thread inherits the creator's signal mask (unless set by attribute), its floating-point environment, and its CPU affinity. It starts with no pending signals and a fresh `errno` and TLS.

**`pthread_exit(v)`** terminates the calling thread. It runs cancellation cleanup handlers, then TLS destructors (§22.6), then makes `v` available to `join`. When the last thread exits, the process exits with status 0.
**`pthread_join(t, &v)`** waits for `t` to terminate and releases it. The `_np` forms try, time out (on `CLOCK_REALTIME`), or time out on a chosen clock.
**`pthread_detach(t)`** means `t`'s resources are released at termination without a join.
**`pthread_self`/`pthread_equal`** identify threads. `pthread_t` values of terminated and released threads may be reused.

**The C11 `thrd_*` functions** have the same semantics with C11 result codes (`thrd_success`, `thrd_nomem`, `thrd_timedout`, `thrd_busy`, `thrd_error`). `thrd_sleep` returns -1 on interruption (with the remaining time) and another negative value on error.
**`__libc_single_threaded`** (2.32) is a `char` that is non-zero while the process has never created a thread. Libraries use it to skip atomic operations.
`EAGAIN`: thread or memory limits.
`EINVAL`: a bad attribute.
`EPERM`: a scheduling policy that is not permitted.
`EDEADLK`: joining self or a join cycle.
`ESRCH`/`EINVAL`: the thread is not joinable. Joining a detached thread, or joining twice, is undefined behaviour.
Build an attribute object that controls a new thread's:
detached state;

stack: size (at least `PTHREAD_STACK_MIN`, which since 2.34 is `sysconf(_SC_THREAD_STACK_MIN)` and not a constant), a caller-provided stack, and the guard size (rounded to pages; 0 disables the guard);
scheduling: policy and parameters, inherited or explicit. Only `PTHREAD_SCOPE_SYSTEM` is supported, and `PROCESS` gives `ENOTSUP`.

CPU affinity and initial signal mask. `pthread_getattr_np(t, &a)` returns the *actual* attributes of a running thread, including its stack bounds. For the main thread, these come from `/proc/self/maps` and `RLIMIT_STACK`. The `_default_np` functions set process-wide defaults. `pthread_{get,set}concurrency` are no-ops kept for XSI. ⚑ HIST.
The `RLIMIT_STACK` soft limit at startup (8 MiB typically), or 2 MiB if that is unlimited.
Request that a target thread terminate.
In the **deferred** mode (the default), the target acts on the request at the next cancellation point (C0.2), or at `pthread_testcancel`.
In the **asynchronous** mode, the target acts at any instruction. Only async-cancel-safe code may run with this enabled.
**Cancellation state** may be disabled, in which case requests stay pending.

**Acting on cancellation** runs the cleanup handlers in LIFO order and TLS destructors. In C++, it unwinds the stack with a forced unwind (`abi::__forced_unwind`). The thread then exits with `PTHREAD_CANCELED`.

If a cancellation point is cancelled *before* the underlying syscall had a side effect, the side effect did not happen. For `close`, the descriptor is still closed (⚑ KERN). For `read`/`write` cancelled after partial transfer, the call returns normally and is not cancelled.
Mutual exclusion. At most one thread owns a mutex.

**Types:** `NORMAL` (self-deadlock on relock), `ERRORCHECK` (`EDEADLK` on relock, `EPERM` on unlock by a non-owner), `RECURSIVE` (a count), and `DEFAULT` (= `NORMAL`). `PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP` spins before blocking.
**Protocols:** `NONE`, `INHERIT` (priority inheritance), `PROTECT` (priority ceiling).
**`pshared`:** usable across processes when the mutex is placed in shared memory.
**Robust:** if the owner dies, the next locker gets `EOWNERDEAD` and must call `pthread_mutex_consistent`. Otherwise, after unlocking, the mutex becomes permanently `ENOTRECOVERABLE`.
**Timeouts:** `timedlock` is absolute on `CLOCK_REALTIME`. `clocklock` (2.30) takes the clock: `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` or `CLOCK_REALTIME`.
**Static initialization:** `PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER` (all zero bytes) and the `_NP` initializers for the other types.
**C11 `mtx_*`:** `mtx_plain`, `mtx_timed`, `mtx_recursive`.
`EBUSY` (trylock), `ETIMEDOUT`, `EDEADLK`, `EPERM`, `EOWNERDEAD`, `ENOTRECOVERABLE`, `EINVAL`, `EAGAIN` (recursion count overflow).

**Condition variables.** `wait(c, m)` atomically releases `m` and blocks until signalled, then reacquires `m`. `signal` wakes at least one waiter, and `broadcast` wakes all. Spurious wakeups are permitted, so callers re-check their predicate. The timed variants use absolute timeouts. The clock is `CLOCK_REALTIME` by default, set by `condattr_setclock`, or given per call (`clockwait`).
**Guarantee (glibc 2.25+):** a signal wakes only a waiter that blocked *before* the signal. Waiters are grouped to ensure this.
⚑ COMPAT: `pthread_cond_*@GLIBC_2.2.5` implement the pre-2.3.2 condvar ABI for old binaries.

**Read-write locks.** Many readers or one writer. The preference is set by `kind_np`: `PREFER_READER` (the default; ⚑ HIST: writer starvation is possible), `PREFER_WRITER_NONRECURSIVE`. A recursive read lock by the same thread is permitted when preferring readers.
**Spin locks.** Busy-waiting mutual exclusion with no blocking. **Kernel:** none.
**Barriers.** Block until `count` threads have arrived. Exactly one of them receives `PTHREAD_BARRIER_SERIAL_THREAD`.
**`pthread_once(&o, fn)`/`call_once`.** Run `fn` exactly once across all threads. Others wait until it completes. If `fn` is cancelled, the once object is reset.
**Keys** are process-wide identifiers. Each thread has its own `void *` value per key (initially NULL), and a key may have a destructor.
At thread exit, destructors run for non-NULL values, repeated up to `PTHREAD_DESTRUCTOR_ITERATIONS` (4) rounds while values remain.
Keys are limited to `PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX` (1024). ⚑ ARB.

**Language-level TLS** (`__thread`, `_Thread_local`, `thread_local`) gives each thread its own instance of a variable. For dynamically loaded modules, the storage is allocated lazily through `__tls_get_addr(module, offset)`.
Static TLS for the executable and initially loaded libraries is at a fixed offset from the thread pointer.
A counting semaphore.
`post` increments and wakes a waiter. It is **async-signal-safe**, the only synchronization primitive that is.
`wait` decrements, blocking while the count is 0. The timed forms take an absolute time.
`getvalue` reports the count (glibc never reports a negative count for waiters).
**Unnamed semaphores** (`sem_init`) are shared between threads or, with `pshared`, between processes.
**Named semaphores** (`sem_open(name, O_CREAT|O_EXCL, mode, value)`) are files in `/dev/shm` named `sem.<name>`. Opening the same name twice in one process returns the same address.
Returns -1 with `errno`: `EAGAIN` (trywait), `ETIMEDOUT`, `EINTR`, `EINVAL`, `EOVERFLOW` (`SEM_VALUE_MAX` = `INT_MAX`), `ENOENT`, `EEXIST`, `EACCES`.
**Naming.** Set or get a thread name of at most 15 bytes plus a terminator (⚑ KERN: `TASK_COMM_LEN` is 16). Returns `ERANGE` if too long.
**Scheduling.** Per-thread scheduling policy and priority.
**`pthread_yield`** is `sched_yield`. ⚑ HIST: it is deprecated.
**Affinity.** A per-thread CPU mask.
**`pthread_getcpuclockid`** returns a clock ID that measures the thread's CPU time.

glibc registers an rseq area for each thread (2.35+, unless disabled with `glibc.pthread.rseq=0`) and publishes its offset from the thread pointer and its size, so that applications can use restartable sequences without registering their own area. `sched_getcpu` reads the current CPU from this area without a syscall.

A library that a *debugger* loads to interpret the thread structures of a target process. The debugger supplies memory and register access callbacks (`ps_pdread`, `ps_pdwrite`, `ps_lgetregs`, `ps_pglobal_lookup`, ...), and the library reports:
the thread list;
the LWP ↔ thread mapping;
TLS addresses;
TSD values;
creation and death event breakpoints.
Return the current value of a clock.
**`clock_gettime(id, &ts)`** reads one of these clocks:
`CLOCK_REALTIME`: settable wall-clock time since the Unix epoch;
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`: not settable; it does not count suspend;
`CLOCK_BOOTTIME`: monotonic including suspend;
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW`: without NTP slewing;
`CLOCK_*_COARSE`: cheaper, lower resolution;
`CLOCK_TAI`;
`CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID`, `CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID`;
dynamic clock IDs: those encoding a PID or TID, and those derived from a PTP clock descriptor.
**`clock_getres`** returns the resolution. **`clock_getcpuclockid(pid)`** returns the CPU clock ID for a process.

**`time(&t)`** returns seconds. **`gettimeofday(&tv, tz)`** returns microseconds; the `tz` argument is obsolete and is filled with zeros. **`ftime`** (compat, removed from the API in 2.33) returns milliseconds. ⚑ HIST: four resolutions of the same need.

**`timespec_get(&ts, TIME_UTC)`** (C11) is `CLOCK_REALTIME`. **`timespec_getres`** (C23) is its resolution. Only `TIME_UTC` is supported in 2.39; the optional C23 bases (`TIME_MONOTONIC`, ...) are not.
**`clock()`** returns the process CPU time in `CLOCKS_PER_SEC` (= 1,000,000) units, or -1. ⚑ HIST: `clock_t` wraps. XSI fixes `CLOCKS_PER_SEC` regardless of the real resolution.

**`times(&tms)`** returns user and system time for the process and for its waited-for children, in clock ticks (`sysconf(_SC_CLK_TCK)` = 100). It also returns an elapsed real-time value in ticks from an arbitrary origin. ⚑ HIST.
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC` never goes backwards. `CLOCK_REALTIME` may jump. `tv_nsec` is always in `[0, 1e9)`.
`EINVAL` (unknown clock), `EOVERFLOW` (32-bit `time_t` ABIs).
**`clock_settime`/`settimeofday`** set a clock. They require `CAP_SYS_TIME`. `settimeofday` with a non-NULL `tz` fails with `EINVAL` in 2.31+ (except for the special `tz`-only call). ⚑ HIST.
**`adjtime(&delta, &old)`** slews the clock gradually by `delta`.
**`adjtimex`/`ntp_adjtime`/`clock_adjtime`** give full access to the kernel NTP state machine (offset, frequency, status, PLL/FLL, TAI offset).
**`ntp_gettime`** reads the time together with the error estimate.
Suspend the calling thread.
**`nanosleep(&req, &rem)`** sleeps for a relative duration on `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`. If interrupted by a handler, it fails with `EINTR` and stores the remaining time.
**`clock_nanosleep(id, flags, &req, &rem)`** sleeps on a chosen clock, relative or absolute (`TIMER_ABSTIME`, which avoids drift). It returns the error number directly.

**`sleep(s)`** returns the unslept seconds (0 if complete). **`usleep(us)`** takes microseconds. ⚑ HIST: `usleep` was removed from POSIX, and it fails with `EINVAL` for `us ≥ 1,000,000` on some systems (not glibc).
Yes.

**`alarm(s)`** schedules a `SIGALRM` after `s` seconds, replacing any previous alarm. It returns the seconds that remained on the previous alarm. It cannot fail. **`ualarm`** does the same in microseconds. ⚑ HIST.

**`setitimer(which, &new, &old)`** sets one of three per-process interval timers: `ITIMER_REAL` (sends `SIGALRM`), `ITIMER_VIRTUAL` (`SIGVTALRM`) or `ITIMER_PROF` (`SIGPROF`). Values are microseconds.
**POSIX timers.** `timer_create(clock, &sigevent, &id)` creates any number of timers per process. Expiry is notified by:
a signal (`SIGEV_SIGNAL`), with `si_value`;
a signal to a specific thread (`SIGEV_THREAD_ID`);
a new thread (`SIGEV_THREAD`, which glibc implements with a helper thread that receives an internal signal);
nothing (`SIGEV_NONE`). `timer_settime` arms the timer, relative or absolute, with a nanosecond interval. `timer_getoverrun` reports expirations missed between signal deliveries.
**`timerfd_*`** are timers that deliver expirations as a readable counter on a descriptor. `TFD_TIMER_CANCEL_ON_SET` notifies when the realtime clock is set.
`EINVAL`, `EAGAIN` (resource limits), `ENOMEM`.

Convert between `time_t` (seconds since the epoch, ignoring leap seconds) and broken-down time (`struct tm`: second 0–60, minute, hour, day of month, month 0–11, year − 1900, weekday, day of year, DST flag, plus the GNU fields `tm_gmtoff` and `tm_zone`).
**`gmtime`** converts to UTC. **`localtime`** converts to the local time zone (§23.6).
**`mktime(&tm)`** is the inverse of `localtime`. It normalizes out-of-range fields (for example day 32 → next month) and resolves `tm_isdst = -1` automatically.
**`timegm`** (2.x, standardized in C23) is the inverse of `gmtime`. **`timelocal`** is an alias of `mktime`. ⚑ HIST.
**`difftime(t1, t0)`** returns `t1 - t0` as `double`.
**`asctime`/`ctime`** produce `"Sun Sep 16 01:03:52 1973\n"`.
**`dysize(y)`** returns 365 or 366. ⚑ HIST.
The `_r` forms write to caller storage. The others return a pointer to a single static `struct tm` or buffer, shared between `gmtime` and `localtime` and overwritten by either (⚑ HIST, ⚑ PATH).
`EOVERFLOW`: the year does not fit an `int`.
`mktime` returns -1 on error. ⚑ HIST, ⚑ ARB: -1 is also the valid time 1969-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, so errors are ambiguous (C23 recommends checking `errno`).

`asctime` has undefined behaviour (ISO C) for years outside 1000–9999. glibc formats years 0 to 9999 (years below 1000 without padding) and returns `NULL` with `EOVERFLOW` for negative years and years above 9999 (⚑ ARB: a fixed 26-byte format). Corrected 2026-10-02 (owner) from black-box observation, `spec/behaviour/zones.md`.
Establish the local time-zone rules from the `TZ` environment variable:
a POSIX rule string (`EST5EDT,M3.2.0,M11.1.0`);
`:path`, or a zone name, resolved as a file under `TZDIR`, default `/usr/share/zoneinfo`;

if `TZ` is unset, the system default `/etc/localtime`. The functions export the standard and daylight abbreviations (`tzname[2]`), the standard offset in seconds *west* of UTC (`timezone`, ⚑ HIST: the sign convention is the opposite of `tm_gmtoff`), and whether DST rules exist (`daylight`).

`localtime`, `mktime` and `strftime` call `tzset` implicitly (or behave as if they did). glibc re-reads the zone file when `TZ` changes, or when `/etc/localtime` changes and `TZ` is unset (checked by `stat`).
**`strftime(buf, max, fmt, &tm)`** formats broken-down time according to a directive language:
ISO C: `%a %A %b %B %c %d %H %I %j %m %M %p %S %U %w %W %x %X %y %Y %Z %%`;
POSIX and C99: `%C %D %e %F %g %G %h %n %r %R %t %T %u %V %z`;
`E` and `O` alternative modifiers (era, alternative digits);

GNU: `%k %l %P %s`, and the flags `_ - 0 ^ #` with width. Names come from `LC_TIME`. It returns the length, or **0 if the result does not fit**. ⚑ HIST, ⚑ ARB: 0 is also the correct length for an empty result, such as `"%p"` in some locales.

**`strptime(s, fmt, &tm)`** parses according to the same directives. It fills only the fields it parses (glibc also computes `tm_wday`/`tm_yday` when possible), and returns a pointer past the consumed input, or `NULL`.

**`getdate(s)`** parses `s` by trying each template in the file named by `DATEMSK`. It returns static storage, with errors in the global `getdate_err` (1–8). **`getdate_r`** returns the error. ⚑ HIST: a global error variable, and configuration through an environment-named file.
Get and set the soft and hard limits for a process resource:
`RLIMIT_AS`, `CORE`, `CPU`, `DATA`, `FSIZE`, `LOCKS`, `MEMLOCK`, `MSGQUEUE`, `NICE`, `NOFILE`, `NPROC`, `RSS`, `RTPRIO`, `RTTIME`, `SIGPENDING`, `STACK`.
`RLIM_INFINITY` means unlimited.
A process may lower its hard limit, and may raise it only with `CAP_SYS_RESOURCE`.
**`prlimit(pid, ...)`** operates on another process.
**`ulimit(cmd, ...)`** is the SVID form: `UL_GETFSIZE` returns 512-byte blocks. ⚑ HIST.

Return the resources used by the process (`RUSAGE_SELF`), by its waited-for children (`RUSAGE_CHILDREN`), or by the thread (`RUSAGE_THREAD`): user and system CPU time, max RSS, page faults, block I/O, and voluntary and involuntary context switches. Several BSD fields are always 0 on Linux. ⚑ KERN.
**`nice(inc)`** adds to the nice value and returns the new value. -1 is a valid result, so the caller must zero `errno`. ⚑ HIST.
**`getpriority`/`setpriority(which, who, prio)`** apply to a process, group or user. ⚑ KERN: the syscall returns `20 - nice` to avoid negative returns, and glibc converts it back.

**Scheduling policies:** `SCHED_OTHER`, `SCHED_BATCH`, `SCHED_IDLE`, `SCHED_FIFO`, `SCHED_RR`. `SCHED_DEADLINE` needs `sched_setattr`, which glibc does not wrap in 2.39. ⚑ KERN: the POSIX functions operate on a *thread* (the TID) on Linux, not on the process.

**Affinity:** `cpu_set_t` masks, 1024 CPUs by default. Dynamically sized sets are available through `CPU_ALLOC`. ⚑ ARB: `cpu_set_t` is 1024 bits, and machines can have more CPUs. ⚑ COMPAT: `sched_setaffinity@GLIBC_2.3.3` versus the older form without a size argument.
**`sched_getcpu()`** returns the current CPU. **`getcpu(&cpu, &node)`** (2.29) also returns the NUMA node.
**`sysconf(name)`** returns runtime values of system limits and options. Examples:
`_SC_ARG_MAX` (a quarter of `RLIMIT_STACK`, at least 128 KiB);
`_SC_CHILD_MAX`, `_SC_CLK_TCK`, `_SC_NGROUPS_MAX`, `_SC_OPEN_MAX`, `_SC_PAGESIZE`;
`_SC_NPROCESSORS_CONF`/`_ONLN`, `_SC_PHYS_PAGES`/`_AVPHYS_PAGES`;
`_SC_LEVEL1_DCACHE_*` (CPUID);
`_SC_MINSIGSTKSZ`, `_SC_SIGSTKSZ`, `_SC_THREAD_STACK_MIN`;
`_SC_GETPW_R_SIZE_MAX`;
about 250 POSIX option names. It returns -1 *without changing errno* for "no limit", and -1 with `EINVAL` for an unknown name. ⚑ HIST: three meanings share one return channel.

**`pathconf(path, name)`/`fpathconf(fd, name)`** return file-system-dependent limits: `_PC_NAME_MAX`, `_PC_PATH_MAX`, `_PC_LINK_MAX` (derived from `statfs.f_type`), `_PC_PIPE_BUF`, `_PC_CHOWN_RESTRICTED`, `_PC_NO_TRUNC`, `_PC_FILESIZEBITS`, `_PC_REC_*`, `_PC_2_SYMLINKS`.
**`confstr(name, buf, len)`** returns configuration Text: `_CS_PATH` (the default `PATH`), `_CS_GNU_LIBC_VERSION`, `_CS_GNU_LIBPTHREAD_VERSION`, `_CS_POSIX_V7_*_CFLAGS`. It returns the full length.
**`get_nprocs()`** counts online CPUs, and **`get_nprocs_conf()`** counts configured CPUs. **`get_phys_pages`/`get_avphys_pages`** count memory pages.
**`uname(&u)`** returns the kernel name, node name, release, version, machine, and domain name (GNU).
**`gethostname(buf, n)`** returns the node name. It fails with `ENAMETOOLONG` if truncated. ⚑ ARB: POSIX allows silent truncation.
**`getdomainname`** returns the NIS domain name, not the DNS domain. ⚑ HIST: a common confusion.

**`gethostid()`** returns a 32-bit host identifier: from `/etc/hostid` if present, otherwise derived from the host's IPv4 address. **`sethostid`** writes `/etc/hostid`. ⚑ HIST: the value is meaningless on modern systems.
**`gnu_get_libc_version()`** returns `"2.39"`, and **`gnu_get_libc_release()`** returns `"stable"`.

**`capget`/`capset`** read and write a thread's capability sets using the kernel's versioned header and data structures (`_LINUX_CAPABILITY_VERSION_3`). They are exported but not declared in any glibc header, and `libcap` is the intended interface. ⚑ HIST.
**`sysinfo(&si)`** returns uptime, load averages, total, free, shared and buffer RAM, swap, process count, and a memory unit.
**`getloadavg(a, n)`** returns up to three load averages, from `/proc/loadavg`.

**`reboot(cmd)`**, **`klogctl`** (the kernel log buffer), **`acct`** (process accounting), **`quotactl`**, **`ioperm`/`iopl`** (x86 port I/O permission), **`vhangup`**, **`init_module`/`delete_module`** and **`modify_ldt`** are thin wrappers.

**`syscall(nr, ...)`** invokes an arbitrary system call by number. It returns -1 with `errno` on error. This is the escape hatch for kernel interfaces glibc does not wrap (`futex`, `openat2`, `sched_setattr`, `io_uring_*`, `bpf`, `perf_event_open`, `clone3`, `landlock_*`, `seccomp`, ...).
The compat entries are stubs failing with `ENOSYS`, or wrappers for syscalls that have been removed from the kernel.
`pipe(fds)` creates a unidirectional byte channel: `fds[0]` reads and `fds[1]` writes. `pipe2` also accepts `O_CLOEXEC`, `O_NONBLOCK` and `O_DIRECT` (packet mode).
Writes of at most `PIPE_BUF` (4096) bytes are atomic.
A read on an empty pipe with no writers returns 0.
A write with no readers raises `SIGPIPE` and fails with `EPIPE`.
The capacity is adjustable with `F_SETPIPE_SZ`.

**Naming.** Kernel-persistent IPC objects named by a numeric key. `ftok(path, id)` derives a key from an inode number, a device number and an 8-bit ID. ⚑ HIST: collisions are possible, and the key space is 32 bits.

**Message queues.** `msgsnd`/`msgrcv` send and receive typed messages. Receive selects by type (the first of that type; for a negative type, the first message of the lowest type up to its absolute value; or any), with `IPC_NOWAIT`, `MSG_NOERROR`, `MSG_EXCEPT` and `MSG_COPY`.

**Semaphore sets.** `semop` performs an *atomic* array of operations on a set. `SEM_UNDO` reverses them at process exit. `semtimedop` adds a timeout. `semctl` is variadic, and its fourth argument is a `union semun` that **the caller must define**. ⚑ HIST.
**Shared memory.** `shmget` creates a segment, and `shmat` attaches it at a kernel-chosen or requested address (`SHM_RND`, `SHM_RDONLY`, `SHM_REMAP`). `shmdt` detaches it.
**Control.** The `*ctl` functions have `IPC_STAT`, `IPC_SET` and `IPC_RMID`, plus Linux-specific info commands.
`EACCES`, `EEXIST`, `ENOENT`, `EIDRM` (removed while waiting), `ENOSPC` (system limits), `E2BIG`, `ENOMSG`, `EAGAIN`, `EINTR`, `ERANGE`.
Named priority queues of messages.
A name is `"/name"`, with exactly one leading slash (⚑ KERN: the `mqueue` file-system namespace).
A message has at most `mq_msgsize` bytes and a priority, and the highest priority is received first.
`mq_notify` requests notification (a signal, or a new thread) when a message arrives on an empty queue, for a single registrant.
Attributes: `mq_flags` (`O_NONBLOCK`), `mq_maxmsg`, `mq_msgsize`, `mq_curmsgs`.

`EAGAIN`, `EMSGSIZE`, `ETIMEDOUT`, `EBADF`, `EINVAL` (a name without the leading slash, or attributes exceeding `/proc/sys/fs/mqueue/*`), `EACCES` (a further slash in the name, or permission denied), `ENOENT` (the name `/` alone, or no such queue without `O_CREAT`), `ENAMETOOLONG` (more than `NAME_MAX` bytes after the slash), `EBUSY` (`mq_notify` is already registered, by any process including the caller: the kernel's rule). Corrected 2026-10-04 (three-way rule: the reference and mq_open(3) agree, `spec/behaviour/posixipc.md`; an earlier text gave `EINVAL` for every bad name).
Send and receive are cancellation points.

Create or open a named shared-memory object. Leading slashes in the name are optional; after them the name is a single component, not `.` or `..`, with no further slash (`EINVAL`; `ENOENT` for `shm_unlink`) and at most `NAME_MAX` bytes (`ENAMETOOLONG`). The result is a descriptor to be sized with `ftruncate` and mapped with `mmap`. `shm_unlink` removes the name. Written 2026-10-04 (owner ruling, phase 12-13 report), `spec/behaviour/posixipc.md`.
**`openlog(ident, option, facility)`** sets a process-wide identifier prefix, options and a default facility. The options are:
`LOG_PID`, `LOG_CONS` (write to `/dev/console` on failure);
`LOG_NDELAY` (connect now), `LOG_ODELAY`;
`LOG_NOWAIT`;
`LOG_PERROR` (also write to stderr).

**`syslog(priority, fmt, ...)`** formats a message (the `printf` language plus `%m`) and sends it to the system logger, prefixed with priority, timestamp and identifier, and with the PID when `LOG_PID` is set (corrected 2026-10-04, three-way rule: the reference and syslog(3) agree, `spec/behaviour/syslog.md`; an earlier text said the PID was always included).
**`setlogmask(mask)`** filters priorities with `LOG_MASK`/`LOG_UPTO`.
**`closelog`** closes the connection.
Messages below the mask are discarded without being formatted.
If the connection fails, the message is retried once after reconnecting.
With `LOG_CONS`, a message that still cannot be delivered is written to the console.
It never reports failure to the caller.
**`dlopen(path, mode)`** loads an ELF shared object and its dependencies into the process and runs their constructors. It returns a handle, and repeated opens are reference-counted.
**Path search** applies when `path` contains no slash: `DT_RPATH`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `DT_RUNPATH`, `/etc/ld.so.cache`, then the default directories.

**Modes:** `RTLD_LAZY`/`RTLD_NOW` (binding time), `RTLD_GLOBAL`/`RTLD_LOCAL` (symbol visibility to later loads), `RTLD_NODELETE`, `RTLD_NOLOAD` (only return an existing handle), `RTLD_DEEPBIND` (prefer the object's own symbols).
**`dlopen(NULL)`** returns the global scope.
**`dlmopen(lmid, ...)`** loads into a separate *link-map namespace* (`LM_ID_NEWLM`), giving an isolated copy of the libraries.

**`dlsym(handle, name)`** returns the address of a symbol. The special handles are `RTLD_DEFAULT` (global lookup order) and `RTLD_NEXT` (the next occurrence after the caller's object, for interposition). **`dlvsym`** requests a specific symbol version.
**`dlclose`** decrements the reference count. At zero, it runs destructors and unmaps the object, unless the object is `NODELETE` or has unique symbols or TLS in use.

**`dlerror()`** returns a Text describing the last failure on this thread, and clears it. It returns `NULL` if there was no error. ⚑ HIST: this is yet another error channel. `dlsym` returning `NULL` is ambiguous for symbols whose value is 0, so callers must check `dlerror`.
**`dladdr(addr, &info)`** / **`dladdr1`** map an address to its object and nearest symbol.
**`dlinfo(handle, request, arg)`** queries a handle: its link map, origin, search paths, TLS module ID and block, and namespace.
**`dl_iterate_phdr(cb, data)`** calls `cb` for each loaded object, with its load address and program headers. The loader lock is held during the callback.
**`_dl_find_object(pc, &res)`** (2.35) finds an object and its `PT_GNU_EH_FRAME` for a program counter without taking locks. It exists for unwinders.
Symbol resolution follows ELF rules (global scope order, symbol versioning, `STB_GNU_UNIQUE`, IFUNC resolvers run at bind time). Constructors run in dependency order.
`NULL` plus `dlerror` text: file not found, wrong ELF class, undefined symbol (with `RTLD_NOW`), static TLS exhaustion, or a version mismatch.

Libraries named in `LD_AUDIT` (or `DT_AUDIT`) receive callbacks from the dynamic linker for library search, object load and unload, symbol binding (they can redirect bindings), and PLT entry and exit.
Return the address of a TLS variable, given a module ID and an offset, for the calling thread. The block is allocated on first access for modules loaded by `dlopen`.
None. Allocation failure aborts the process. ⚑ ARB: there is no error channel for a lazy allocation.

`_r_debug` and `_dl_debug_state` implement the debugger rendezvous. The debugger sets a breakpoint on `_dl_debug_state` and walks the `r_debug.r_map` list after each change. Since 2.35 `r_version` is 2, which adds a linked list of namespaces.

Report CPU features as detected by the dynamic linker (CPUID plus OS support via XCR0, masked by `glibc.cpu.hwcaps` tunables): "present" means the CPU supports the feature, and "active" means it is also usable.
**`monstartup(lowpc, highpc)`** allocates histogram and arc tables for a text range and starts PC sampling. `_mcleanup` writes `gmon.out` (or `$GMON_OUT_PREFIX.<pid>`) at exit.
**`mcount`/`_mcount`** is called at every function entry of `-pg` code and records the call arc.
**`profil(buf, size, offset, scale)`** samples the PC into a histogram on every `ITIMER_PROF` tick. **`sprofil`** takes multiple regions.
**`__cyg_profile_func_enter/_exit`** are empty hooks called by `-finstrument-functions` code, for the application to interpose.
`__fentry__` is the profiling counter call that `-pg -mfentry` code makes before the function prologue; it records the call arc as `mcount` does (§28.1). The others are covered in their sections.
**XDR** serializes C data to and from the External Data Representation (RFC 4506): encode, decode and free, for primitive types, arrays, strings, unions, pointers, and record-marking streams.
**The RPC runtime** provides client handles over UDP, TCP and Unix sockets, server dispatch, portmapper registration, and authentication flavours (`AUTH_NONE`, `AUTH_UNIX`/`AUTH_SYS`, `AUTH_DES`).
Client functions for Sun's Network Information Service (`yp_match`, `yp_first`, `yp_next`, `yp_all`, `yp_order`, `yp_master`, `yp_get_default_domain`, `yp_bind`, ...) and for NIS+.
None. These always fail with `ENOSYS`. `isastream` returns 0 for valid descriptors. ⚑ COMPAT: they were added for XSI conformance. Linux never implemented STREAMS.
Each keeps the contract it had when it was removed. Most are aliases of current functions, or stubs that fail with `ENOSYS`. Three are special:
**`__libc_freeres()`** releases all of libc's internal allocations so that leak checkers (Valgrind) report cleanly.
**`__libc_malloc` and friends** are aliases of `malloc` that cannot be interposed.
**`sysctl`/`__sysctl`** fail with `ENOSYS`, because the kernel removed the syscall in 5.5.
